(I am not talking about Honor of Kings itself, of course, but about a brainless player like this editor. Boo-hoo! Have you ever suffered through nineteen consecutive losses? Do not follow my example and grow accustomed to being reported.) Instead, Laws face support or resistance from different Interest Groups. Those groups may be pursuing private gain, or the livelihoods of a million grain-transport workers may depend on the issue.

  Interest Groups on either side bring their Clout to bear and compete with one another. The stronger the opposition, the more likely a reform is to become mired in argument and stagnation. For example, if the Qing Scholar-Officials have too much Clout, changing the education system so that private academies focus primarily on science becomes very difficult. Workers may want an eight-hour day while capitalists demand a twelve-hour one. Amid this endless exploitation, capital in the game rivals capital in real life.

  (Here are a few examples everyone will recognize. At Foxconn, national regulations prescribe an eight-hour workday and treat anything beyond it as overtime. Yet the company uses twelve-hour shifts that rotate between night and day. I experienced this firsthand during the winter break of my first year at university. It was hell on earth and a miniature version of the game. Having looked at the bottom tier, consider the middle: Huawei, nicknamed the “Chrysanthemum Factory,” should be familiar to everyone. I had the chance to intern there in my second year. “996” may be only a label; more than two-thirds of the time, the schedule was 9 a.m. to 11 p.m., a full fourteen hours. Yes, really. Some people will say the pay is high, and it certainly is… But that is not our focus. The point is to introduce the appeal of the game. I think students of politics, management, and finance will enjoy the Victoria series.)

(Figure 5: Victoria gameplay screenshot)

  In the game, the player acts as the ruler, holding supreme power but also bearing the greatest responsibility and mission: serving the people, promoting labor laws, and enabling people to live in peace. Because wealthy capitalist interest groups wield excessive influence, however, labor laws can be difficult to pass. The game lets players experience the enormous efforts that historically late-industrializing countries made to protect their domestic industries during the early stages of industrialization. At times, it feels less like a game than a miniature version of reality.

  In many games, technology simply means domestic development and strength, and building a factory immediately produces money. The Victoria series does not portray modern industrialization so simplistically. Its ideas are more advanced because they draw on both our past and our present. Different buildings have different statistics and effects, allowing the game to simulate populations more realistically. To operate, for example, a factory needs raw materials, workers, and customers. From the workers’ perspective alone, inadequate education may leave the factory unable to recruit enough literate employees. Independent farmers with stable lives may be so accustomed to that stability that they refuse factory work no matter how high the wages. If production exceeds demand and the products cannot be sold, the factory may also fail after exhausting its cash reserves.

  The Victoria series sold poorly and received a lukewarm response when it first appeared. Perhaps because of the era, the series was discontinued. Later, as time passed, the world economy recovered, and education in China gradually improved, more players discovered the games’ distinctive framework and central ideas, and the series slowly gained recognition.

Victoria’s materialist view

  Compared with Paradox’s earliest titles, Victoria II no longer constructs its world according to a historical timeline. Instead, it tries to uncover the logic behind history. If Britain had not done so, could another feudal country have become the first to complete an Industrial Revolution by resolving its own problems? After the Industrial Revolution, everyday goods became scarcer than ever before, the population surged, and advancing industrialization put large numbers of artisans out of work. Might that country have begun migrating to the New World in the Americas before Britain to solve its population problem? The Industrial Revolution also produced too many goods. When a crisis emerged, might this country have sought to resolve it by dumping those goods (The Opium War of 1840 was Britain’s attempt to dump goods into China), then gone to war with a self-sufficient country that had not completed a modern industrial revolution? Once the world market had been fully divided, might imperialist wars have broken out among industrial countries? The game’s distinctive framework and materialist conception of history contain a fascinating internal logic that builds a complete virtual world.

Advice for readers who want to play Victoria

  Victoria 3 is now available. It makes detailed changes to the earlier games, such as reducing their historicity, leaning further toward today’s diverse society, and fixing known bugs. The results are quite good. I am an engineering student who has played Victoria for three years. If your budget is tight, I suggest waiting before buying it, because it is rather expensive. Another option is to look for a “mirrored” version on certain shopping or secondhand platforms.

  All right, that is the end of this installment!!

entry.title: Traditional Chinese Philosophy: A Brief Lecture
entry.content:
Author: Silicon-Based
Reviewer: Xian’e

  I drafted this lecture while my school was locked down during the pandemic. I had already reached the library’s borrowing limit, and all the books I had annotated were at my home far away in southern China. I wrote almost entirely from my not especially reliable memory, so this account of traditional Chinese philosophy is bound to contain substantial omissions and mistakes. Please approach it cautiously and critically.

  By traditional Chinese philosophy, I generally mean the systems of Chinese thought, sometimes grouped under “Eastern philosophy,” that dominated the intellectual life of East Asia from the Hundred Schools of Thought in pre-Qin China until Marxism entered the country. Compared with its counterpart, “Western philosophy,” traditional Chinese philosophy has many distinctive features. It gives greater weight to moral injunctions and social forms than to the systems and methods of natural science; emphasizes unity over particularity; values people over things; accepts the real existence of a supreme order and seeks harmony between human beings and the external world; and shows a strong tendency toward elementary dialectical thought. More than a thousand years of practice under feudal society shaped what we now call the “spirit of the Chinese nation” and left modern China with immense cultural inertia. Studying this tradition can help readers understand China’s present intellectual landscape and trace contemporary social and cultural phenomena to their roots.

  Traditional Chinese philosophy first took recognizable form in the pre-Qin era, during the Hundred Schools of Thought. Before then, ancient China had a primitive philosophy made up of early beliefs and moral ideas: the seed from which the later tradition grew. As the productive forces developed, the slaveholding relations of production under the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties, along with their political and cultural superstructure, reached the limits those forces imposed. More advanced feudal relations of production called for more centralized authority. The result was the prolonged and frequent warfare of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, which destabilized society and badly damaged production. In that turbulent age, advanced thinkers reflected on the sparse philosophy of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou, systematized it, and developed it into many outstanding schools of thought.

  Among the landowning ruling class, perceptive rulers in different regions recognized that the unsystematic ideas inherited from the past could no longer meet the demands of government, development, and the struggle for supremacy. Confucianism, Legalism, the School of Military Strategy, and the School of Diplomacy supplied political philosophies suited to those demands and formed communities of shared interest with the ruling class. At this stage, each side supported the other and helped it advance.

  For ordinary people, social upheaval dealt a severe blow to both production and daily life. Their straightforward desire for solidarity combined with their advanced productive forces and, under the leadership of the brilliant Mozi, produced an organized, disciplined, and united proto-political collective: the Mohist school. Meanwhile, the desire of peasants and rulers alike to restore production, together with advances in agriculture, gave rise to the technically oriented philosophy of the Agriculturalist school.

  Because Mohism and Agriculturalism answered concrete needs created by the development of the productive forces, they produced early forms of technology and science. Then there was Daoism… Childlike ideals inherited from primitive morality collided with the harsh reality of social turmoil, leaving Laozi, a minor official, with a profound spiritual void. He felt both the desire to “withdraw from the world” and the ideal of “engaging with the world.” Out of this contradiction came a remarkably early philosophy with tremendous reach. From the vantage point of the supreme principle, the “Dao,” it built new systems of morality and knowledge. By taking a position beyond its own age, it escaped the immediate moment and found spiritual grounding in the eternal and the vast (“Heaven and earth are not humane; they treat the myriad things as straw dogs”). Zhuangzi later inherited these moral and cognitive systems and used them to build a philosophy of self-exploration and an inner world of freedom. Other schools, including the School of Names, the Yin-Yang School, the School of Minor Talks, and the Miscellaneous School, served different classes and groups. They were less independent: some were absorbed through continued conflict and exchange with larger schools, while others eventually declined into purely technical fields of knowledge. Even so, their independent thinking and defiant posture in debate did much to mature and develop early Chinese philosophy, and their historical contribution was considerable.

  By the late Warring States period, hard-line philosophies of rule, chiefly Qin Legalism and military thought, had achieved great success in maintaining stability and contesting supremacy through force and violence. That success led the ruling class, the Legalists, and military strategists to make a serious mistake: they assumed that the philosophy and methods of a period of intense struggle could be applied directly to government and reconstruction once the contest for rule was over. The Qin dynasty accordingly fell after only two emperors. The collapse dealt a severe blow to the School of Military Strategy, which ceased to be an independent philosophical school and became an abstract, technical body of knowledge. The clearest sign of the shift is that later periods had plenty of “generals” but very few “military thinkers.” Legalism, meanwhile, could not satisfy the ruling class’s growing demand for centralized power and was reshaped and absorbed by Han Confucianism. Most other schools met a similar fate, epitomized by the call to “suppress the Hundred Schools and exalt Confucianism alone.” Only Daoism, grounded in a deeper and more expansive supreme order, retained a degree of independence. Even it was driven by political and academic pressure to merge with ancestral worship and develop into an unusual phenomenon in religious history: religious Daoism.

  The chaos in which the Hundred Schools of Thought had flourished did not end until Qin unified the country. Through the burning of books and burying of scholars, Qin Shi Huang developed a tool of centralized rule that represented the new relations of production: “unified thought.” After Qin fell, Liu Bang won popular support by rejecting its harsh Legalism in his “Three Rules of Law.” He did not, however, give up the basic principles of “unified thought” and “centralized authority.” Stable government in a country as large and populous as China made them inevitable. Qin’s failure also alerted the ruling class to the disastrous consequences of mistaken ideas and helped prompt Dong Zhongshu’s “suppression of the Hundred Schools” during the reign of Emperor Jing of Han. In practice, the various schools were critically absorbed and recombined into a more complete “New Confucianism.” Confucianism already served the ruling class, and the new synthesis better met its need for centralized power. It retained the basic framework of moral education, benevolent rulers, and mutual care between ruler and people, while incorporating Legalist and Daoist insights that helped stabilize rule. The result was a social order that served the long-term shared interests of the ruling class and Confucian scholars. This successful intellectual transformation sustained the exceptionally long rule of three Han reigns and placed Confucianism at the center of Chinese philosophy for the next thousand years.

  Confucianism presupposed a monarchy. Its reforms focused on the ruler, who was expected to practice “benevolent government,” and they held up an ethical model and ideal: the junzi, or “exemplary person.” This ideal was used to teach people a social morality in which “the ruler is a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, and the son a son.” The original logic of Confucian government ran as follows: “The ruler practices benevolent government and loves the people; the people will in turn love a benevolent ruler. Moral education and ritual music teach the people, while family ethics arrange social relations and organize production. Initiated from above, this creates a stable top-down society in which everyone occupies the proper place.”

  Under Dong Zhongshu’s reforms, Confucianism kept morality at its core while incorporating useful methods and ideas from many other schools. It adopted, for example, the Legalist use of written law to limit a ruler’s power and regulate social customs, as well as the Daoist policy of rest and recovery when production had been badly damaged. This expanded form of Confucianism protected the ruling class’s hold on power more effectively.

  Confucianism sought to preserve the stability of feudal society primarily through moral instruction, emotional norms, and ties of blood. When it came to the productive forces and relations of production, however, its outlook went no further than the reactionary and passive policy of “emphasizing agriculture and suppressing commerce.” This was an inevitable limitation.

  Because Confucianism made “emphasizing agriculture and suppressing commerce” an important principle of rule, China’s bourgeois class developed extremely slowly. The broader structure of philosophical thought remained at the level of feudal society for a long time, with no major breakthroughs. During the Wei, Jin, and Northern and Southern dynasties, scholar-officials faced political darkness and social turmoil by turning to Daoism for spiritual support. Out of this turn came the Wei-Jin school of xuanxue, or “arcane learning.” More generally, the pattern was Confucianism in orderly times and Daoism in troubled ones.

  By the Tang dynasty, rulers continued to support the Buddhist thought that had developed since the Northern and Southern dynasties. Buddhism flourished, adding a distinctive and powerful new current to the old contest between Confucianism and Daoism. The Tang commercial economy grew, politics remained stable, and its rulers were clear-minded; government and culture prospered as a result. China was then a global center of culture, where innumerable ideas and religions met in the East. Chang’an even housed a Zoroastrian fire temple, which gives some sense of the era’s cultural splendor.

  In this age of cultural exchange, Chinese philosophy reached a turning point. Material life was growing richer, and a bourgeois class was beginning to emerge; under the pressure of the times, new ideas collided and took shape. Through the successive periods of turmoil from the Southern dynasties to the Sui and early Tang, Buddhism’s transcendent worldview of rebirth, reincarnation, and the gathering and dispersal of karmic conditions offered comfort amid real hardship. Its beautiful picture of the afterlife won followers who were suffering in the present. Rulers differed sharply in their attitudes toward Buddhism. Some believed in it, and under them it expanded dramatically, at times producing the spectacle of “one temple, one cooking pot, a hundred monks.” Yet an excessively large religious community did not engage in productive labor. This held society back and created a corrupt alliance of religion and politics. Other rulers recognized Buddhism’s drawbacks or followed a traditional reverence for antiquity and rejection of foreign influences. They launched campaigns to “eradicate” or “ban” Buddhism, repeatedly forcing it to submit to political power. Before the Tang, this uneven development gave Buddhism a broad popular base while also compelling it to adapt to China. During Wu Zetian’s reign, the emergence of Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of Chan, definitively marked the completion of Buddhism’s Sinicization. Buddhism as a religion had also become “Buddhist philosophy.”

  Daoism changed from an intellectual and political force into a religious one. Buddhism followed the opposite path in China. It arrived as a religion, then gradually moved beyond that identity through a difficult process of localization and became an intellectual force within Chinese philosophy. The clearest evidence is that one can read Buddhist scriptures without being a Buddhist, accept and apply their knowledge and wisdom, and find ideas in them that the Confucianism and Daoism of the time did not offer.

  Buddhism initially brought China a radically different otherworld. There was no register of gods decreed by Jiang Ziya; instead, anyone could practice and become a Buddha. Nothing in this life was accidental; there was only the necessity of reincarnation. Most importantly, Buddhism placed human suffering and the means of ending it at the center of its thought. Everything, including suffering, was an empty appearance. Material things came together and dispersed according to causes and conditions, while the spirit passed through cycles of reincarnation. Material needs, or desire, were described as the source of all suffering and as meaningless attachments. Buddhist philosophy therefore made “the emptiness of the four elements” its highest aim, while practice meant “breaking attachments” and “breaking through appearances.” Once even “attachment to the self” had been broken, the self itself could cease to exist. One could then enter a transformed state of pure spirit and return to the most innocent, lucid, compassionate, and benevolent condition: “Originally there was not a single thing; where could dust alight?”

  The various Buddhist schools differ mainly in how they interpret the scriptures and conduct their practice. Their broader values are consistent.

  Buddhism and Daoism are similar in temperament, but they differ in essential ways. However far Daoism withdraws from society and seeks purity and stillness, its central concern remains the problems of this world. What matters most is living freely here and now. It neither defers happiness and prosperity to an illusory otherworld nor denies the existence of the self. Before Buddhism was Sinicized, its faith in the otherworld and the attainment of Buddhahood was unwavering. Records even describe groups of monks meditating on high mountains until they died of hunger and cold. Such practices were wholly at odds with China’s secular traditions.

  As Buddhism became Sinicized, it therefore grew less religious and more secular. The famous story of Wang Yangming “persuading an old monk to return to lay life” reflects this process. We may struggle to understand the existence of “Buddhist extremists” in India today precisely because the Buddhism familiar to us has long been Sinicized and secularized. Comparing it with the Esoteric tradition of Tibetan Buddhism, which developed in relative isolation from the culture of the Central Plains, supports the same conclusion.

  Traditional Chinese Confucian and Daoist philosophy is ultimately concerned with this world. “The Master did not speak of strange phenomena, feats of strength, disorder, or spirits,” and not one sentence in the Dao De Jing discusses another world, the underworld, or the origins of life and death. These philosophical systems are not inherently religious. Superstition and ancestral worship later produced religious concepts such as the “underworld,” “Lingxiao Palace,” “Supreme Lord Lao,” and the “Jade Emperor.” Even these ideas grew out of older forms of worldly moral instruction. Like heaven and hell in the West, they were intended to regulate behavior in this life. Consequently, Confucian and Daoist philosophy could not offer scientific explanations for certain basic questions, such as the “origin of the spirit” or the “essence of human beings.” They either avoided such questions or resorted to mystery. To understand Chinese philosophy properly, we must separate out its religious elements when examining its actual ideas, yet include those elements when considering the limits of its thought.

  The arrival and Sinicization of Buddhist philosophy therefore addressed transcendent questions that Confucianism and Daoism had neglected or left unanswered, while also introducing a new set of values. Laozi’s Dao De Jing itself remains rooted in the real-world images of the “ruler,” “people,” “water,” and “infant.” Like Confucianism, it could not escape politics. From their beginnings, both Confucianism and Daoism were closely tied to the ruling class’s needs in government, and the systems they formed could not in practice be separated from politics. For the ruling class, both were ultimately forms of learning directed toward political ends, which is why they endured throughout feudal society. Ordinary people had no need for such learning. If they pursued it, they did so to sit examinations and become officials, which still amounted to the ruling class preserving itself.

  Buddhist philosophy, by contrast, could separate itself from politics and spread among ordinary people. It addressed spiritual needs regardless of class and used religious means to comfort the population at large. Chan Buddhism in particular taught that one could “see one’s nature and become a Buddha” and relied on “no written words,” greatly lowering the barrier for ordinary people to study Buddhist thought. Once Sinicized, Buddhism could also provide the social and moral instruction the ruling class needed. By the Tang, a Chinese philosophical system centered on “Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism” had begun to take shape. After this round of conflict and integration, and propelled by the developmental needs of the bourgeoisie, Chinese philosophy was ready to enter a new stage.

  During the Song and Ming dynasties, Zhou Dunyi, Zhu Xi, the Cheng brothers, and the Lu-Wang school moved Confucian-centered Chinese philosophy forward considerably. Confucianism developed in two broad directions during this period. One was a further extension of the highly systematized union of scholarship and politics: Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism. The other combined Buddhist and Daoist ideas and brought philosophy back to the people: the Lu-Wang School of Mind.

  Traditional Chinese philosophy was essentially mature by this stage. The philosophy developed by Huang Zongxi and others who represented new bourgeois currents had taken on certain modern features, including political ideas such as “democratic demands” and the “free market.” Its basic methods remained within the bounds of traditional Chinese philosophy, an inevitable limitation, although the thought itself did move beyond the conventional system. My knowledge is too limited for me to reach a sound conclusion, so I will leave the subject there.

  The central figures of Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism were the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi. They carried forward earlier Confucian learning and emphasized “orthodoxy.” Academic opinion of the school is relatively low today, but to the ruling class it was an almost ideal instrument of ideological control. It represented a nearly perfected form that emerged as intellectuals and the ruling class adapted to one another within a community of shared interests. The Neo-Confucianism reshaped by these three thinkers advocated “preserving heavenly principle and extinguishing human desires,” pushing moral discipline to an extreme. The results included the oppression of women through such ideals as the so-called “chaste martyrs” and “chastity arches,” as well as horrifying stories such as “Guo Ju Buries His Son” in The Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars. Zhu Xi’s Collected Commentaries on the Four Classics also allowed “revering the ancient and rejecting the new” and strained interpretation to flourish in later ages. This was probably why Li Zongwu once concluded: “Western learning was simple at first and then grew increasingly rigorous and complete; Chinese learning began at an extremely high level and then became progressively worse.” Although Neo-Confucian scholars controlled moral judgment, the scholar-official class itself often lived dissolutely, until its halls eventually filled with hypocrites. The Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi were accomplished moral thinkers and scholars. Yet the survival and development of their intellectual synthesis ultimately depended on its alliance of interests with the ruling bloc, and an autocratic feudal monarchy was bound to become corrupt. No number of great Cheng-Zhu scholars could save it.

  The Lu-Wang School of Mind, especially Wang Yangming’s thought, can be called Confucianism’s final high point. It truly absorbed the best ideas of Buddhist philosophy and Daoism, although Wang himself denied doing so, and brought a Confucianism that appealed to the “Way of Heaven” back to human beings, the human mind, and subjective agency. Here, “human beings” meant not only the scholar-official class but every person in the fullest sense. Emperors, kings, generals, and ministers had to study Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism, yet they found it tiresome. It was a body of thought distorted by the alliance between Neo-Confucianism and imperial power. It alienated people by stripping human life of its value and assigning that value to an elusive “Way of Heaven”: for the sake of that Way, your life counted for nothing. Wang Yangming, however, proposed that “the mind is principle.” Heavenly principle was not an abstract, external, eternal object in some other realm that only a handful of sages could master. It existed in the “mind” of everyone, from emperors and generals to porters and common laborers. Morality arose from the human mind. It was neither external nor dictated by sages; it belonged to you. This was a Confucian philosophy for the people. It still revolved around the central ideas of “morality” and “benevolence,” but its character had changed fundamentally. First, “the mind is principle,” like “seeing one’s nature and becoming a Buddha,” greatly lowered the barrier to entry. It genuinely addressed ordinary people’s desire to learn instead of being kept out of reach and serving only the ruling class. This explains the esteem and warm welcome Wang received among the people of his time. Second, “the mind is principle” did away with an external and abstract “Way of Heaven.” What remained was morality arising from within. There was no “Way of Heaven” apart from concrete human beings and no external Other that could impose such a Way on you; the “Way of Heaven” was in your own mind. This restored to human beings the meaning that the Way had taken from them. It emphasized subjective agency and the effect of individual will on collective will. In this sense, Wang Yangming’s breakthrough somewhat resembled Marx’s dialectical transcendence of Feuerbach. Yet traditional Chinese philosophy, centered on Confucianism, had long depended on a scholar-official class that did not engage in production. Its ideas were never made precise through practice and scientific expression, and it never developed a rigorous scientific methodology. In the end, what separated it from Marx was its lack of scientific rigor.

  In the Qing dynasty that followed, centralization reached its height and brought even tighter control from the center. Literary inquisitions and restrictions on thought nearly halted the development of Chinese philosophy, while selecting officials through the “eight-legged essay” uprooted any basis for traditional philosophy to develop under the Qing. Only when the rumble of modern artillery drew near and Western ideas gradually entered China did the country’s intellectual world begin another round of breakthroughs. By then, however, it had moved beyond the domain of traditional philosophy.

  The seeds of ancient, primitive morality were scattered across China. As the climate warmed and rain grew plentiful, the Hundred Schools of Thought sprouted everywhere. After a long and fierce struggle, only two trees, Confucianism and Daoism, grew tall. Confucianism claimed the richest soil and water. It flourished, tall and luxuriant, though its wood was soft. Defiant Daoism grew from bare rock at the edge of a cliff. It was neither tall nor thick, and its leaves were sparse, but it was hard and resilient. For thousands of years, the seasons turned. In fair weather, birds gathered in the Confucian tree; in harsh weather, they huddled in the Daoist one. Then, during a particularly lovely spring, a bird from far away brought a seed called Buddhism. Unlike other short-lived, stunted seeds, Buddhism grew wildly as soon as it took root in the Central Plains. Botanists said that a metabolic waste product neither the Confucian nor the Daoist tree could recycle had accumulated in the soil, and that this waste happened to be ideal fertilizer for Buddhism. To keep Buddhism from overgrowing and taking its ecological niche, Confucianism repeatedly crowded it until its growth was checked. Through conflicts large and small, the three great local trees came to be known collectively as Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism. As the soil grew richer and the climate improved, all three kept growing and competing. They discovered that each could learn from the others and take what it needed. Through competition and cooperation, the three trees grew strong and formed a harmonious ecological relationship. That, in broad outline, is how the community called “traditional Chinese philosophy” evolved.

  [End of Part One: A Historical Overview of Traditional Philosophy]

entry.title: The ‘Fixed’ Stars Aren't Fixed: How Their Positions Change
entry.content:
Author: Congyu
Reviewer: Baiyan

  With excellent eyesight, you might pick out more than 2,500 stars on a clear, dark night. Across the entire celestial sphere, nearly 6,000 are visible to the naked eye. Ancient observers noticed that, unlike the five planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, most celestial objects seemed to keep the same positions forever. That apparent permanence gave us the Chinese word for star, which literally means “constant star.” We now know that stars only look fixed: they are so distant that their motion across the celestial sphere is hard to detect. This article introduces three ways their positions shift against the celestial background:

  • Parallax
  • Proper motion
  • Aberration of light

Parallax

  Hold up a finger and look at it first through one eye, then the other. Against the background, your finger plainly jumps from one position to another. That is parallax: the difference in an object’s apparent direction when it is observed from two locations. The line between those observing points is the parallax baseline, and the angle between the two sight lines is the parallax angle. Once we know that angle, finding the distance is a straightforward exercise in triangle geometry—hence the name trigonometric parallax.

  As Earth revolves around the Sun, its changing position supplies the two viewpoints needed for stellar parallax. Because the Earth–Sun distance is known, we can use the mean distance of 1 AU as the baseline; the result is called annual parallax. Stars are so far away that the parallax π in Figure 1 is extremely small, so tan π ≈ π. Find a baseline in the plane of Earth’s orbit—the ecliptic plane—perpendicular to the direction of the star, and its distance follows: d = a / π. By definition, an object whose annual parallax is 1 arcsecond (″) lies 1 parsec (pc), or approximately 3.262 light-years, away. This convenient definition has made the parsec one of astronomy’s standard units of distance: simply take the reciprocal of the annual parallax in arcseconds to get the distance in parsecs. Since parallax shrinks with distance, it works accurately only for relatively nearby targets. Even so, the Gaia telescope, which entered service in 2013, can measure to roughly 10 microarcseconds and detect stellar parallaxes thousands of parsecs away.

Annual stellar parallax

  For any given star, the line from the Sun to the star generally meets the ecliptic plane at an angle. In heliocentric ecliptic coordinates, that angle is the star’s ecliptic latitude β. As Earth moves around its circular orbit, the sight line from Earth to the star traces an ellipse on the celestial sphere. For a star on the ecliptic, that annual-parallax track collapses into a line; near the north ecliptic pole, it becomes a circle. The semimajor axis of the parallax ellipse equals the annual parallax and corresponds to the parallax baseline. Thanks to symmetry, observations spanning any six months are enough to reconstruct the full ellipse and calculate the star’s distance.

The parallax ellipse of a star in space

  Parallax measures more than stars beyond the Solar System; it also works for objects inside it. During a transit of Venus, for example, observers at two places on Earth see Venus at different points on the Sun’s disk. From that difference, they can calculate Venus’s distance and orbital radius. Even the Sun shows parallax when viewed from different parts of Earth. With Earth’s radius as the baseline, solar parallax is approximately 8.8″.

Proper Motion

  The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way. Suppose a star’s velocity relative to the Sun is v. We can resolve it into two perpendicular components: radial velocity v_r and tangential velocity v_t. The tangential component points in the direction we see the star move, while proper motion μ describes the size of that apparent movement, usually in arcseconds per year.

A star’s space velocity and proper motion

  Once we know a star’s proper motion and distance, its tangential velocity is easy to calculate. Add a measurement of radial velocity, and we have its true velocity through space relative to the Sun. Radial velocity comes from the Doppler effect: motion changes the wavelengths emitted by a light source. A receding source shifts toward longer wavelengths—a redshift—while an approaching source shifts toward shorter ones—a blueshift. Comparing lines in a star’s spectrum with their rest wavelengths therefore reveals both the magnitude and direction of its radial velocity.

  Barnard’s Star has the greatest known proper motion. The red dwarf lies approximately 6 light-years away and crosses the celestial background at 10.3″ per year. Figure 3 shows its changing position between 1985 and 2005.

The proper motion of Barnard’s Star

Aberration of Light

  Because light has a finite speed, a moving observer sees it arrive from a different direction than a stationary observer does. This effect is called the aberration of light. Think of walking through rain: although the drops fall straight down, a runner sees them slanting in from the front. Light behaves similarly, except that we must use the Lorentz transformation rather than the classical addition of velocities.

  Earth never stops moving. It rotates, circles the Sun, and travels with the Sun through the Milky Way. Each motion produces aberration when we observe a distant light source. The largest effect in practice is annual aberration from Earth’s revolution. In Figure 3, θ is the angle between the direction of motion and the light source. Earth’s motion changes the observed angle to φ, making the aberration θ - φ.

Direction of motion and the aberration of light

  Earth travels around the Sun at approximately 29.8 km / s. When a speed v is far below the speed of light c, the aberration is simply v sin θ / c. With the velocity perpendicular to the incoming light, annual aberration reaches its maximum of 20.5″. Diurnal aberration from Earth’s rotation is two orders of magnitude smaller. Aberration from the Solar System’s motion around the Milky Way is larger, but its period is so long—200 million years—that we can ignore it over short timescales.

  Like parallax, annual aberration makes a star trace a one-year ellipse as Earth’s direction of motion changes. Depending on the star’s ecliptic coordinates, that track ranges from a circle to a straight line segment. Its maximum swing of 20.5 arcseconds is far larger than stellar parallax. Parallax, proper motion, and aberration overlap, making a star’s path across the celestial sphere look tangled and irregular. Fortunately, their periodic, systematic behavior lets us separate and analyze their effects.

entry.title: Automotive Styling and Aerodynamics
entry.content:
Author: 未名
Reviewer: 未名

Introduction

  In 1886, Karl Benz built the world’s first three-wheeled automobile powered by an internal-combustion engine. What chiefly distinguished it from a horse-drawn carriage was its powertrain; the basic form of the modern four-wheeled car came from Daimler. Over the next century and more, vehicle bodies evolved along with the demand for greater mobility and changing aesthetic tastes. From the Beetle to the ponton body and then the wedge shape, designers have pursued forms that reduce drag without sacrificing visual appeal. This article briefly examines the relationship between automotive styling and aerodynamics.

Automotive Styling and Aerodynamic Drag

  At constant speed on a level road under normal atmospheric pressure, a car's aerodynamic drag consists of pressure drag and skin-friction drag. Depending on the relative contribution and the part of the vehicle involved, this drag can be classified as form drag, induced drag, roughness and interference drag, or internal-flow drag. About 69% of a car's fuel is used to overcome air resistance, and form drag accounts for 58% of its aerodynamic drag. Body shape is therefore critical to reducing resistance. The drag coefficient is defined as Cw=F_drag/(ρ/2 v_∞² A), where v_∞ is the velocity of the vehicle relative to the uniform airflow far upstream, and A is its frontal area. Figure 1-1 compares the drag coefficients of several vehicle shapes moving at the same constant speed through the same horizontal, uniform, ideal airflow. The differences among them are substantial.
Figure 1-1
  We will now consider each type of aerodynamic drag in turn.

Form Drag

  Pressure drag accounts for 80–90% of a car's form drag, while skin friction contributes only 10–20%. Figure 1-2 illustrates the pressure drag on several shapes in the same ideal fluid:
Figure 1-2
  On a bluff body, such as a flat plate set across the flow or a rectangular block, pressure rises sharply near the largest cross-section. The flow then separates and forms a vortical wake behind the body. The resulting asymmetric pressure distribution over the surface produces pressure drag. Rounding an edge can delay or prevent separation as the flow passes it, thereby reducing pressure drag. The same principle applies to cars.
  Now consider skin-friction drag:
Figure 1-3
  The velocity gradient and molecular viscosity within the boundary layer produce wall shear stress τw at every point on the surface. The sum of the components of this stress in the direction of flow is the skin-friction drag.
  When the flow remains attached, friction can account for a large share of the total drag; when extensive separation occurs, its share is much smaller. This is why dimples help a golf ball travel farther. On a streamlined body, including some vehicles, skin-friction drag makes up a relatively large proportion of the total.
  All liquids and gases are viscous. When adjacent fluid parcels move at different speeds, friction acts between them. Viscosity also causes the fluid next to a solid surface to adhere to it. This fluid slows the layers moving past it, forming a boundary layer that produces frictional drag. A laminar boundary layer interacts less strongly with the surface than a turbulent one, so it produces less frictional drag and absorbs less energy. On a streamlined body, friction therefore accounts for a comparatively large share of the total drag.
  A car therefore needs a smooth surface finish.

Induced Drag

  Induced drag arises from the pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces of the body, although it is not itself lift. This pressure difference adds a vertical component to the horizontal freestream. Air moves around the sides of the body to equalize the pressure, generating vortices that travel downstream. Producing these vortices continuously consumes energy and therefore creates induced drag. Induced drag is related to aerodynamic lift, as discussed below.
Figure 2-1. Induced drag around a car

Roughness and Interference Drag

  Roughness and interference drag include the resistance caused by surface discontinuities and accessories that protrude through the boundary layer around the car. Chassis and suspension components, wheels, mirrors, auxiliary lights, and windshield wipers all contribute.
  Interference drag may be positive or negative, with opposite effects on total resistance. Positive interference drag arises between nearby or connected objects. A side mirror, for example, disturbs the car's original flow field, causes earlier separation, and increases aerodynamic drag. Negative interference drag occurs because every object in a flow leaves a region of slower-moving fluid behind it. A second object placed within that region experiences less resistance than it would in undisturbed flow. For example, when two discs are aligned at a suitable distance, their combined drag is lower than the sum of the drag on each disc tested separately (Figure 2-2). The same principle applies to tractor-trailers: an aerodynamically optimized tractor can reduce the combination's overall drag.
Figure 2-2

Internal-Flow Drag

  Internal-flow drag, also called internal drag, is produced as air passes through the vehicle for engine cooling and ventilation. It includes momentum losses at the outlet and pressure losses through the radiator and engine compartment, both of which consume additional energy. Internal-flow drag accounts for about 5–12% of total aerodynamic drag.

Automotive Styling and Aerodynamic Lift

  A car's aerodynamic lift arises from its shape (Figure 3-1).
Figure 3-1
  Under ideal conditions, Bernoulli's equation gives:
  Applied to the shape of a car, this gives, under ideal conditions:
F_top ＜ F_bottom
  The result is an aerodynamic lifting force.
  In practice, the underbody also matters. Figure 3-2 shows simplified two-dimensional inviscid and viscous flows, along with the pressure distributions around a car:
Figure 3-2
  A car's rolling resistance is proportional to the normal force on its wheels. Increasing aerodynamic lift reduces that force and therefore reduces rolling resistance. At first glance, lift might seem to lower the vehicle's total resistance. Greater lift, however, also reduces traction and stability while producing additional induced drag that may far exceed the reduction in rolling resistance. Using lift to reduce drag is therefore a poor tradeoff. A large increase in lift compromises high-speed stability and creates a safety hazard. Above 70 km/s, for example, some cars may begin to feel “light” as aerodynamic instability reduces the driver's sense of contact with the road, potentially contributing to a rollover or skid.
  This led to the wedge-shaped car. These aerodynamically optimized bodies, most commonly found on sports cars, may also use spoilers to generate downforce. Their aerodynamic lift can even be negative, greatly improving stability at high speed.

(Some of the text and figures in this article draw on Aerodynamics of Road Vehicles.)

entry.title: The Philosophy and Theology of Saint Augustine
entry.content:
The Philosophy and Theology of Saint Augustine

Author: Михaїл-А-Булгáкoв☦️
Reviewed by: 观复·钧天

  Saint Augustine was an extraordinarily prolific writer whose works dealt mainly with questions of theology. His polemical writings addressed the issues of his day and, once they had served their purpose, generally lost all significance. Some of them, however, especially those concerning the Pelagians, have continued to exert a real influence into modern times. I do not intend to cover everything he wrote. Instead, I will examine the works and arguments that seem to me important in themselves or in their historical influence:
  • First, his pure philosophy, especially his theory of time
  • Second, the philosophy of history presented in The City of God
  • Third, the theory of salvation developed in opposition to Pelagianism

Pure Philosophy

  Saint Augustine did not, in general, devote himself single-mindedly to pure philosophy, but when he did engage with it, he displayed exceptional ability. Many thinkers throughout history have allowed the demands of scriptural conformity to shape their speculative views, and Augustine stands at the head of that long line. This was not yet true of early Christian philosophers such as Origen. In Origen's writings, Christianity and Platonism coexist without penetrating each other. In Augustine's work, by contrast, original philosophical thought was stimulated by the tension between Platonism and *Genesis*.
  Among Saint Augustine's writings, Book XI of Confessions is his finest work of pure philosophy. Some popular editions of *Confessions* contain only ten books, since the material after Book X is considered dull. It is dull precisely because it is no longer autobiographical and instead contains a great deal of philosophy. Book XI addresses this question: if creation occurred as described in the first chapter of *Genesis*, as Augustine maintained against the Manichaeans, why did it not happen sooner? He imagines an opponent raising this objection and develops his argument in response.
Excerpt from *Confessions*
  To understand this discussion, one must first recognize that the Old Testament idea of creation out of nothing was wholly foreign to Greek philosophy. When Plato spoke of creation, he imagined God giving form to primordial matter; Aristotle held a similar view. Their God was less a creator than a designer or architect. They believed matter to be eternal and uncreated, with only its form arising from the will of God. Against this view, Saint Augustine maintained, as every orthodox Christian had to, that the world was created not from any preexisting matter but out of nothing. God created matter itself; he did not merely order and arrange it.
  The Greek conviction that nothing could be created from nothing resurfaced intermittently during the Christian era and gave rise to pantheism. Pantheism holds that God and the world cannot be distinguished and that everything in the world is part of God. This view was fully developed in the writings of Spinoza and appealed to almost every mystic. Throughout the Christian centuries, mystics had difficulty remaining orthodox because they found it hard to believe that the world existed outside God. Augustine had no difficulty on this point. *Genesis* was perfectly clear, and that was enough for him. His position had important consequences for his theory of time.
  Why was the world not created sooner? Because there was no “sooner.” Time was created along with the world. God is eternal in the sense of existing outside time: in God there is no before and after, only an eternal present. God's eternity is independent of temporal relations; for God, all time is present. He did not precede the time he created, for that would mean that he himself existed in time. Instead, God stands eternally outside the stream of time. This led Augustine to formulate a highly admirable theory of the relativity of time.
  “What, then, is time?” he asked. “If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know.” Several difficulties perplexed him. What really exists, he said, is neither the past nor the future, but only the present. Yet the present is merely an instant, while time can be measured only as it passes. Even so, past and future time plainly do exist, leaving us with an apparent contradiction. Augustine found only one way around it: the past and future can be conceived only as present. The “past” must be identified with memory, and the “future” with expectation; memory and expectation are both facts that exist now. He said there are three times: “a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future.” “The present of things past is memory; the present of things present is sight; the present of things future is expectation.” (To speak simply of three times—past, present, and future—is merely a loose expression.)
  He also understood that this theory did not solve every problem. “My mind longs to understand this most intricate riddle,” he wrote. He prayed that God would enlighten him and assured God that his concern did not arise from idle curiosity. “Lord, I confess to you that I still do not know what time is.” The central point of his answer, however, is that time is subjective: “Time exists in the mind that expects, attends, and remembers.”
  Thus, if there were no created beings, there could be no time; it is therefore meaningless to speak of time before creation.
  I do not agree with this theory, which makes time a product of the mind. It is nevertheless plainly remarkable and deserves serious consideration. I would go further: it is a great advance on any theory of time found in Greek philosophy. Its account is also more complete and explicit than Kant's subjective theory of time, a theory widely accepted by philosophers since Kant.
  The view that time is merely an aspect of thought is an extreme form of subjectivism. As we have seen, subjectivism had grown gradually in antiquity since the age of Protagoras and Socrates. Its emotional side was an obsession with sin, though this developed later than its intellectual side. Saint Augustine advanced two forms of subjectivism that made him a precursor not only of Kant's theory of time, but also of Descartes' “I think” (cogito). In his Soliloquies, Augustine wrote: “You who wish to know—do you know that you exist? I know it. Where do you come from? I do not know. Do you think yourself simple or composite? I do not know. Do you think that you move? I do not know. Do you know that you think? I know it.” This passage contains not only Descartes' cogito, but also Gassendi's reply, “I walk, therefore I am” (ambuloergosum). Augustine accordingly deserves a high place as a philosopher.

The City of God

  When Rome was sacked by the Goths in 410 CE, pagans naturally blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the ancient gods. Rome had remained powerful, they said, while it worshiped Jupiter. Now that the emperors no longer worshiped him, he no longer protected the Romans. This pagan argument demanded an answer. The City of God, written in stages between 412 and 427, was Saint Augustine's response. As the work progressed, however, its scope expanded until it became a complete Christian account of past, present, and future history. It exerted enormous influence throughout the Middle Ages, particularly in the Church's struggles against secular rulers. Like some other great works, it leaves a better impression in the reader's memory than it does upon rereading. Much of its content is unacceptable to any modern reader, and its central thesis is obscured by matters of little importance today. Yet the broad contrast between the earthly city and the City of God has continued to inspire many people, so much so that it can still be restated in non-theological terms.
The first page of a manuscript of *The City of God*, written in 1470
  Any introduction to this work that omits the details and concentrates on its central idea will praise it too highly. An account that concentrates on the details, however, will inevitably miss its finest and most important features. I will try to avoid both errors by first describing some of those details and then discussing its general ideas in the order of their historical development.
  The book begins with reflections prompted by the sack of Rome and tries to show that even worse events had occurred before the Christian era. Pagans often blamed disasters on Christianity, the saint says, yet many of them sought refuge in churches during the sack. The Gothic invaders were Christians and respected those churches. When Troy was sacked, by contrast, Juno's temple failed to shelter the people, and the gods did not protect the city from destruction. The Romans had never spared the temples of conquered cities, yet Rome received comparatively lenient treatment when it was sacked, and Christianity was responsible for that leniency.
  For several reasons, the Christians who suffered during the sack had no right to complain. Wicked Goths might enrich themselves at the Christians' expense, but they would suffer in the next life. If every sin were punished on earth, there would be no need for the Last Judgment. If the Christians were virtuous, their suffering must strengthen their virtue. To a saint, losing worldly possessions means losing nothing of value. Even if their bodies received no burial, it did not matter, for ravenous beasts could not prevent the resurrection of the flesh.
Two Gothic soldiers
  He then turns to the rape of devout virgins during the sack. Some evidently believed that these women had lost the crown of virginity through no fault of their own. Saint Augustine rejected this view very sensibly. “Away with the thought! Another person's lust cannot defile you.” Chastity is a virtue of the mind and cannot be lost through rape; a sinful intention, even if never carried out, can cause its loss. He suggests that God permitted these rapes because the victims had been excessively proud of their continence. Suicide to escape rape is sinful. This leads to a long discussion of Lucretia, who, in his view, should not have killed herself, since suicide is always a sin.
  His defense of virtuous women who have been raped includes one reservation: they must not have enjoyed it, or they are guilty.
  He next discusses the wickedness of the pagan gods. “Those stage plays of yours, those displays of filth, those licentious pagan deities, were not first introduced into Rome by human corruption; they arose by the direct command of your gods.” Worshiping a virtuous man such as Scipio would be more edifying than worshiping these immoral gods. Christians need not be troubled by the sack of Rome, because they have a refuge in “God's pilgrim city.”
  In this world, the two cities, the earthly city and the heavenly city, are intermingled. In the next world, God's predestined elect will be separated from the reprobate. In the present life, we cannot know who, even among those who appear to be our enemies, will ultimately prove to be one of the elect.
  He tells us that the most difficult part of the book is its refutation of the philosophers, since Christians and certain eminent philosophers agree to a considerable extent, for example on the immortality of the soul and the doctrine that God created the world.
  The philosophers did not renounce belief in the pagan gods, but since those gods were wicked, their moral teaching was worthless. The book does not suggest that the pagan gods were merely fictions. Saint Augustine believed they existed, but that they were all demons. They wished to harm humankind and were therefore willing to spread obscene stories about themselves. For most pagans, Jupiter's deeds were more influential than Plato's principles or Cato's opinions. “Plato excluded poets from a well-governed city; this shows that he himself was worthier than the gods who wished to be honored with stage plays.”
  He says that Rome had been thoroughly wicked ever since the Romans raped the Sabine women. Augustine devotes several chapters to the grave sins of Roman imperialism. The claim that Rome never suffered before becoming Christian is false: its sufferings during the Gallic invasion and the civil wars equaled or exceeded those inflicted by the Goths. Astrology is not merely wicked but false, as shown by the different fates of twins born at the same moment. The Stoic view of fate, which is connected with astrology, is wrong because angels and human beings possess free will. God foreknows our sins, but we do not sin because he foreknows them. The idea that virtue brings misfortune, even in this world, is likewise false. Virtuous Christian emperors are happy even when they encounter adversity; Constantine and Theodosius were both quite fortunate. Moreover, the Jewish kingdom endured for as long as the Jews remained faithful to religious truth.
Statue of Constantine the Great
  The book contains a passage highly sympathetic to Plato, whom Augustine ranks above every other philosopher. All philosophers, he thinks, should yield to Plato: “Let Thales depart with his water, Anaximenes with the air, the Stoics with fire, and Epicurus with his atoms.” All these thinkers were materialists; Plato was not. Plato held that God is not a corporeal thing, but that all things derive their being from God and from something constant and immutable. He was right that perception is not the source of truth. The Platonists excelled in logic and ethics and came closest to Christianity. “Plotinus, who lived not long ago, is said to have understood Plato best.” Aristotle, though inferior to Plato, stood far above the other philosophers. Yet both Plato and Aristotle said that all the gods were good and deserved worship. The Platonists were right about God but wrong about the other gods, and they were also wrong not to acknowledge the Incarnation.
  Saint Augustine opposed the Stoic condemnation of every passion. A Christian's passions, he held, might become causes of virtue; anger and pity should not be condemned in themselves. We must examine what causes them.
  The book includes a lengthy discussion of angels and demons connected with the Neoplatonists. Angels may be good or evil, but demons are always evil. For angels, knowledge of worldly things, though they possess such knowledge, is base. Both Saint Augustine and Plato considered the sensible world inferior to the eternal world.
  Book XI begins its account of the nature of the City of God, the society of the elect. Knowledge of God can be obtained only through Christ. Some things, as certain philosophers demonstrate, can be discovered by reason, but for all further religious knowledge we must rely on Scripture. We must never try to understand the time and space before the world was created: there was no time before creation and no space where there was no world. Everything blessed is eternal, but not everything eternal is blessed; hell and Satan, for example, are eternal. God foresaw the sins of the demons, but also their role in improving the universe as a whole, rather like an antithesis in rhetoric.
  Origen was wrong to think that bodies were given to souls as punishment. If that were so, evil souls would have evil bodies. Yet demons, including the most wicked demons, have ethereal bodies, which are superior to our own.
  God created the world in six days because six is a perfect number—that is, it equals the sum of its proper divisors.
  There are good angels and bad angels, but even bad angels have no nature contrary to God. They are God's enemies not by nature but by will. An evil will has no efficient cause, only a deficient cause; it is not an effect but a defect.
  Fewer than six thousand years have passed since creation. History is not cyclical, as philosophers suppose: “Christ died for our sins only once.”
  If our first parents had not sinned, they would not have died. Because they did sin, all their descendants must die. Eating the apple brought not only natural death but also eternal death, that is, everlasting punishment. Porphyry was wrong to believe that the saints in heaven have no bodies. The saints will have bodies better than Adam's before the Fall. Their bodies will be spiritual, but not spirits, and will have no weight. Men will have male bodies and women female bodies; those who died in infancy will be resurrected with adult bodies.
  Adam's sin brought eternal death—everlasting punishment—to almost all humankind, but God's grace rescues many from it. Sin comes from the soul, not the body. The Platonists and the Manichaeans were both wrong to blame sin on bodily nature, though the Platonists' error was less grave than that of the Manichaeans. The punishment imposed on all humanity for Adam's sin was just, because that offense reduced beings who might have possessed spiritual bodies to minds ruled by carnal desire.
  This question leads to a long and tedious discussion of sexual desire. According to Augustine, our subjection to lust forms part of the punishment for Adam's sin. The discussion is important for what it reveals about ascetic psychology, so it must be summarized. Although Saint Augustine himself admits that the subject is absurd, we must discuss it for the same reason. His doctrine is as follows. Sexual intercourse within marriage must be considered innocent when undertaken to produce children. Yet even within marriage, a virtuous person cannot manage it without lust. The fact that people wish to conceal intercourse shows that they consider it shameful even in marriage, because “this lawful act of nature has, since our first parents, been accompanied by the shame of sin.” The Cynics believed that no one ought to feel shame. Diogenes wished to free himself from shame completely and behave like a dog in every respect, but after trying once, even he abandoned such extreme shamelessness in practice. Lust is shameful because it is not subject to the will. Before the Fall, Adam and Eve might have had intercourse without lust, though in fact they did not. Craftsmen feel no lust when moving their arms to perform their work; likewise, had Adam stayed away from the apple tree, he might have performed the sexual act without the emotions now required. The sexual organs might have obeyed the will like every other part of the body. The need for lust in intercourse is one punishment for Adam's sin. Otherwise, sexual desire and pleasure might have gone their separate ways. Apart from certain physiological details, which the English translator of this book judiciously left in the appropriate obscurity of the original Latin, this is Saint Augustine's theory of sexual desire.
  The ascetic's aversion to sexual desire plainly arises from its refusal to obey the will. Morality requires the will to control the body completely, but such control would make the sexual act impossible. Sexual activity therefore appears incompatible with a morally perfect life.
  After Adam's sin, the world was divided into two cities. One would reign eternally with God; the other would suffer everlasting torment with Satan. Cain① belonged to the city of the devil, Abel to the City of God. By divine grace and predestination, Abel was a pilgrim on earth and a citizen of heaven. The twelve patriarchs also belonged to the City of God. A discussion of Methuselah's death led Augustine into the disputed comparison between the Septuagint and the Latin Bible. According to the Septuagint's chronology, Methuselah must have lived for fourteen years after the Flood. That was impossible, since he had not entered Noah's Ark. The Latin Bible, following the original Hebrew, records that Methuselah died in the year of the Flood. Saint Augustine concluded that Saint Jerome and the Hebrew text must be right on this point. Some claimed that hostility toward Christians had led the Jews to falsify the Hebrew Bible deliberately, but Augustine rejected this hypothesis. On the other hand, the Septuagint must also have been divinely inspired. The only possible conclusion, therefore, was that Ptolemy's copyists had made an error while copying it. Discussing the various Old Testament translations, Augustine wrote: “The Church has accepted the Septuagint as though no other translation existed, just as many Greek Christians know only this version and do not know whether there is another. Our Latin version was likewise translated from the Septuagint. Yet a learned monk and great linguist, Jerome, translated this Bible directly from Hebrew into Latin. Although the Jews confirmed the accuracy of his accomplished translation and said that the Septuagint contained many errors, the churches of Christ judged that no single man should be preferred to those many translators, especially since the high priest had chosen them for this task.” He accepted the story that the seventy translators worked separately yet arrived at a miraculous agreement, regarding this as evidence that the Septuagint was inspired by the Holy Spirit. But the Hebrew Bible was equally inspired. That conclusion left the authority of Jerome's version unresolved. Augustine might have sided more decisively with Jerome had the two saints not quarreled over Saint Peter's tendency toward duplicity.
Palma il Giovane — Cain and Abel
  Augustine compared the chronologies of sacred and secular history. By his account, Aeneas arrived in Italy while Othniel was judge in Israel. The final persecution would be led by the Antichrist, though its date was unknown.
  After an admirable chapter opposing judicial torture, Saint Augustine refuted the New Academics, who believed that everything should be doubted. “Because the Church of Christ possesses the most certain knowledge of the things it understands, it rejects these doubts as madness.” We ought to believe the truth of Scripture. He went on to argue that there can be no true virtue apart from true religion. Pagan virtue is “defiled by the power of obscene demons.” What is virtue in a Christian becomes vice in a pagan. “Some things which she [the soul] regards as virtues and on which she prides herself, if they are not entirely related to God, ought in truth to be called vices rather than virtues.” Those outside this society—the Church—will suffer eternal misery. “In the struggles of our present life, either suffering conquers and death then drives away the capacity to feel it, or nature conquers and drives suffering away. But there, suffering will torment forever and nature will suffer forever. Both will endure an unending punishment.” (Chapter 28).
  There are two resurrections: the resurrection of the soul after death and the resurrection of the body at the Last Judgment. After discussing the difficulties surrounding Christ's thousand-year reign and the subsequent actions of Gog and Magog①, Augustine turns to a passage in 2 Thessalonians (Chapter 2, verses 11 and 12): “God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: that they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.” It might seem unjust for an omnipotent God first to deceive them and then punish them for being deceived, but Saint Augustine saw nothing surprising in this. “They are deluded because they have been condemned, and condemned because they have been deluded. Yet their delusion comes from the secret judgment of God, a judgment at once secretly just and justly secret, which he has continued since the creation of the world.” Saint Augustine believed that God divides people arbitrarily into the elect and the reprobate, not according to human merit. Everyone equally deserves eternal punishment, so the reprobate have no grounds for complaint. The passage from Saint Paul quoted above suggests that people are wicked because they are reprobate, rather than reprobate because they are wicked.
  It is not surprising that, after the resurrection of the body, the bodies of the condemned will burn without end yet never be consumed; salamanders and Mount Etna provide examples. Demons, though incorporeal, can be burned by corporeal fire. The torments of hell do not purify people and cannot be reduced through the intercession of the saints. Origen was wrong to think that hell was not eternal. Heretics and deeply sinful Catholics will suffer everlasting punishment.
  The book ends with Saint Augustine's vision of God in heaven and the eternal happiness of the City of God.
Modern artistic cover of The City of God
  The preceding summary may not yet make the work's importance clear. One influential feature is its separation of Church and State, with the definite implication that a State can form part of the City of God only by submitting to the Church in every religious matter. This claim thereafter remained a principle of the Church. Throughout the Middle Ages, during the gradual rise of papal power and the successive conflicts between popes and emperors, Saint Augustine provided the theoretical basis for the Western Church's policy. The Jewish state was a theocracy both in the legendary period of the Judges and in the historical period after the return from Babylonian captivity. Christian states should imitate it in this respect. The weakness of Roman emperors and most medieval rulers in Western Europe greatly helped the Church realize the ideal of the City of God. No such development occurred in the Eastern Roman Empire, where the emperors were strong and the Eastern Church was far more subordinate to the State than the Western Church.
  The Reformation, which revived Saint Augustine's doctrine of salvation, rejected his theocratic theory and moved toward Erastianism, mainly because of the practical demands of its struggle against Catholicism. Protestant Erastianism, however, lacked fervor, and the most religious Protestants remained under Saint Augustine's influence. The Anabaptists, Fifth Monarchy Men, and Quakers inherited part of Augustine's doctrine but placed less emphasis on the Church. Augustine upheld predestination while also maintaining that baptism was necessary for salvation. These two principles do not fit together very well, so some radical Protestants abandoned the latter. Their eschatology nevertheless retained Augustine's principles.//①Erastianism is the doctrine that the Church must submit to the State.
  *The City of God* contains very little original theory. Its eschatology came from the Jews and entered Christianity chiefly through the Book of Revelation. Predestination and the doctrine of the elect are Pauline, though Augustine developed them more fully and logically than Saint Paul's epistles had done. The distinction between sacred and secular history is already explicit in the Old Testament. Augustine merely combined these elements and related them to the history of his own time, enabling Christians to adapt to the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the chaotic period that followed without putting their faith through too severe a trial.
  The Jewish way of understanding past and future history has always appealed powerfully to the oppressed and unfortunate. Saint Augustine applied it to Christianity; Marx applied it to socialism. To understand Marx psychologically, we should use the following dictionary:

Yahweh = dialectical materialism; Messiah = Marx; the elect = the proletariat; the Church = the Communist Party; the Second Coming = the revolution; hell = punishment of the capitalists; Christ’s thousand-year reign = the communist commonwealth

  The terms on the left carry the emotional content of those on the right. This emotional content, long familiar to Christians and Jews, gave Marx's eschatology the value of a faith. A similar dictionary could be drawn up for the Nazis, but their concepts were closer to the Old Testament and less close to Christianity than Marx's. Their Messiah resembled the Maccabees more than Christ.

The Pelagian Controversy

  The most influential part of Saint Augustine's theology arose from his attack on the Pelagian heresy. Pelagius was Welsh; his original name was Morgan, meaning “man of the sea,” which is also the meaning of the Greek word “Pelagius.” He was a mild and courteous monk, not a fanatic like many of his contemporaries. He believed in free will, questioned the doctrine of original sin, and held that human virtue resulted from people's own moral effort. If people behaved properly and belonged to the orthodox faith, they would enter heaven as a reward for their virtue. Although these views sound commonplace today, they caused a major upheaval at the time and were declared heretical largely because of Saint Augustine's opposition. For a time, however, they enjoyed considerable success. Augustine had to write to a church elder in Jerusalem, warning him against this cunning founder of a heresy who had persuaded many Eastern theologians to adopt his mistaken views. After Augustine's condemnation, a group known as the Semi-Pelagians advocated Pelagian doctrine in a milder form. Augustine's relatively pure doctrine did not win a complete victory until much later, especially in Gaul, where Semi-Pelagianism was finally condemned as heresy at the Council of Orange in 529 CE.
  Saint Augustine taught that Adam possessed free will before the Fall and could have avoided sin. But when he and Eve ate the apple, moral corruption entered them and was inherited by all their descendants. Those descendants could no longer avoid sin through their own power. Only God's grace could make a person virtuous. Because we have all inherited Adam's original sin, we all deserve eternal punishment. Everyone who dies unbaptized, even an infant, goes to hell and suffers endless torment. Since we are all wicked, we have no right to complain. (In *Confessions*, Saint Augustine lists the sins he committed in infancy.) Yet through God's freely given grace, some of the baptized will be admitted to heaven. These are the elect. They do not enter heaven because they are good; all of us are corrupt except insofar as God's grace, granted only to the elect, saves us from corruption. There is no reason why some are saved while the rest are damned. It is simply God's unmotivated choice. Eternal punishment demonstrates God's justice; salvation demonstrates his mercy. Both equally display his goodness.
Adam and Eve eating the forbidden fruit
  Arguments supporting this cruel doctrine can be found in the writings of Saint Paul, especially the Epistle to the Romans. The doctrine was revived by Calvin and has since been abandoned by the Catholic Church. Augustine treated these writings as a lawyer treats the law. His interpretation was powerful, and he pressed the text for every possible implication. One is ultimately led to suppose that Saint Paul's faith was not quite what Augustine inferred, though certain passages, taken in isolation, do suggest Augustine's meaning. The claim that the eternal punishment of unbaptized infants, far from being horrifying, comes from a benevolent God may seem preposterous. Yet Augustine was so deeply ruled by a conviction of sin that he genuinely regarded newborn babies as limbs of Satan. Many exceptionally cruel features of the medieval Church can be traced to Augustine's dark sense of universal guilt.
  Only one intellectual difficulty truly troubled Saint Augustine. It was not the thought that creating humanity might have been regrettable because most people were destined for eternal torment. What troubled him was this: if original sin, as Saint Paul taught, was inherited from Adam, then the soul, like the body, must be generated by the parents, since sin belongs to the soul rather than the body. He found this doctrine difficult. But because Scripture never addressed the question, he concluded that a correct view of it could not be necessary for salvation and left the matter unresolved.
  It is truly strange that the last outstanding intellectuals before the beginning of the Dark Ages, rather than concerning themselves with preserving civilization, expelling the barbarians, or reforming political abuses, enthusiastically preached the value of virginity and the eternal punishment of unbaptized infants. Once we understand that these were among the prejudices the Church passed on to converted barbarians, however, it becomes easy to see why the following age surpassed almost every recorded period in cruelty and superstition.

entry.title: Procedural Art: Drawing a Black-and-White Checkerboard with Code
entry.content:
Author: Shiguang
Reviewed by: Dongda

  Many readers probably first encountered “procedural art” in an elementary-school information technology class, when a textbook introduced the fascinating program Turtle Graphics. Think back: how did we make the little turtle move? The answer was code. In 1996, Seymour Papert and Wally Feurzeig invented Logo, a language designed to teach children programming, and we used it to direct a turtle around the screen as it drew. As technology has evolved, however, Logo has gradually faded from view, and mainstream approaches to drawing have changed as well.
  This article shows how to use a shader language—called simply Shader below—to draw a 3*3 checkerboard. I use UE4 for the demonstration. If you are interested, try the algorithm presented here in Unity or on an online rendering site such as ShaderToy.
  Why begin a series on procedural art with a checkerboard? It is one of the more basic procedural-art exercises: the algorithm is straightforward, and the result is easy to work out. That makes it approachable for readers who are interested in Shader but do not know it well. Because the article does involve some technical terms, however, it is recommended for readers with some background in computer graphics. With that said, let's get started.

Getting Started

  Open UE4's powerful Shader Graph and get ready to draw. First, connect the texcoord node—a set of texture coordinates—to base color on the output root node. The result looks like this:


  What exactly are we looking at, and where did it come from? (It really does look like some kind of fruit.) First, remember that the texcoord node stores a set of texture coordinates ranging from 0 to 1. If we take the upper-left corner of the rectangle in Figure 1 as the origin and point the y-axis downward, the texcoord coordinate (0, 0) refers to the upper-left corner, while (1, 1) refers to the lower-right.
