These include a small storm erupting before the main storm and clearing its path; the storm being reflected by a coronal hole, causing the magnetic field to accumulate; and a sustained sequence of flares in which later eruptions catch up with earlier ones, creating intense shocks and regions of compressed magnetic field within the storm. When these conditions align perfectly, Earth can experience a once-in-a-century solar storm. Humanity would need four to ten years to recover from such an event.

  Although solar storms are among the most violent forms of space weather, they are not the whole story. Space weather also includes the quiet solar wind; interaction regions between high- and low-speed solar-wind streams, where the high-speed streams emerging from coronal holes carry fast charged particles and a strong interplanetary magnetic field and become another major cause of geomagnetic storms and other severe space weather; the heliospheric current sheet; and cosmic rays from beyond the Solar System. If we are “fortunate” enough to witness a supernova in our lifetimes, we may even receive a dose of space weather from a distant star.

  As the discussion above shows, our space environment is far from calm. Hidden currents surge beneath its surface, and at times towering, turbid waves rise around us. What keeps the small ship of Earth moving steadily through this turbulent, dark ocean—and has even allowed fragile life to evolve aboard it and become aware of it all? Earth’s magnetic field. Without that field, the roaring solar wind would quickly strip away the atmosphere. Liquid water would cease to exist, and life would be out of the question.

  Where, then, does Earth’s magnetic field come from? Its liquid metallic core. If that core solidified, Earth’s magnetic field would quickly weaken to a negligible level. Why is the core liquid? Because heat released by the decay of radioactive elements warms it. Where did those radioactive elements come from? Scientists generally believe that they came mainly from collisions between binary neutron stars. Why do neutron stars collide? Because the gravitational waves they emit carry away orbital energy, drawing their orbits closer together. Why do gravitational waves exist? Because general relativity predicts them. We should therefore understand why we live in a world where general relativity holds: if it did not, Earth would have no magnetic field to protect us, space weather could take away everything on which we depend at any moment, and we could not still exist today.

  When I began writing, I never expected a discussion of space weather to lead from the tip of Einstein’s pen to the rise and fall of humanity. That is precisely what reveals the breathtaking beauty of science and reminds us to explore and to think: When humanity thinks, God laughs; but if humanity does not think, God cannot even be bothered to laugh.

entry.title: Deep-Sky Object Catalogs: A Brief Guide
entry.content:
Author: 丛雨

The Messier Catalog

  Of all the deep-sky catalogs, the Messier Catalog is probably the best known. Compiled under the direction of French astronomer Charles Messier, it contains 110 deep-sky objects: 12 nebulae (M1, the Crab Nebula, is its only supernova remnant), 57 star clusters (28 globular and 29 open clusters), 40 galaxies, and one double star, M40, included by mistake. Many favorites among amateur astronomers are Messier objects, including the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Orion Nebula (M42), and the Pleiades (M45). Messier himself was a dedicated comet hunter. While searching for comets, he kept encountering objects that looked like them but were not, so he compiled a catalog first published in 1771. That original list contained 45 objects. By 1781, observations by Messier and Pierre Méchain had expanded it to 103, and later astronomers added the remaining entries. Because Messier observed from France, he could not survey the entire sky; all Messier objects therefore lie north of roughly −36° declination. The catalog is especially well suited to observers in the Northern Hemisphere. Around late March each year, many amateur astronomers choose a clear, moonless night for a “Messier marathon,” trying to find every object with a telescope in a single night.

Messier objects

The Caldwell Catalog ©

  The Caldwell Catalog is less famous than the Messier list. It contains 109 relatively bright deep-sky objects from both the northern and southern skies, none of which appears in the Messier Catalog. The list comprises 25 nebulae, including two supernova remnants, one dark nebula, and 13 planetary nebulae; 43 star clusters; 35 galaxies; and six combined cluster-and-nebula objects. British amateur astronomer and science writer Sir Patrick Caldwell-Moore compiled the catalog in 1995. Better-known entries include the Double Cluster in Perseus (C14) and the Hyades in Taurus (C41). It also includes southern objects that may be less familiar to northern observers, such as the Carina Nebula (C92) and the globular cluster 47 Tucanae (C106). Because Caldwell was designed to complement Messier, none of its objects has an M number, and vice versa. Many of its southern targets are difficult for observers in the Northern Hemisphere to see in full.

Caldwell objects

New General Catalogue of Nebulae and Clusters of Stars (NGC)

  Apart from Messier numbers, NGC designations are probably the deep-sky identifiers we encounter most often. The catalog contains 7,840 nebulae, star clusters, and galaxies, and nearly every familiar deep-sky object has an NGC number. The Andromeda Galaxy, for example, is both M31 and NGC 224. The earliest NGC data came from observations at Dunsink Observatory by William and John Herschel and other members of the Royal Astronomical Society. John Dreyer first organized and compiled the material in 1880. Because the original data contained some errors, later astronomers checked and corrected it several times, producing works such as the Revised New General Catalogue (RNGC).

Index Catalogue of Nebulae and Clusters of Stars (IC)

  Usually called the Index Catalogue, the IC extends and supplements the NGC with another 5,386 objects. It consists of IC I and IC II, completed by Dreyer in 1895 and 1905, respectively. The Horsehead Nebula in Orion (IC 434) is one familiar IC object. An object does not have both an NGC and an IC designation.

  Beyond these four common catalogs, astronomers use many others for galaxies, nebulae, and star clusters. Here are a few of them:

  • Uppsala General Catalogue (UGC): 12,921 galaxies, almost all in the northern sky
  • Catalogue of Galaxies and Clusters of Galaxies (CGCG)
  • Morphological Catalogue of Galaxies (MCG)
  • Principal Galaxies Catalogue (PGC): includes both the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds
  • Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies (Arp): 338 morphologically unusual galaxies, including galaxies undergoing collisions and mergers
  • Sharpless catalogue of bright nebulae (Sh2): 313 emission nebulae
  • RCW Catalogue: 180 emission nebulae, mainly in the southern sky
  • Gum Catalogue: 85 emission nebulae, mainly in the southern sky
  • Lynds’ Catalogue of Bright Nebulae (LBN) and Lynds’ Catalogue of Dark Nebulae (LDN)
  • van den Bergh Catalogue of Reflection Nebulae (vdB): 158 reflection nebulae
  • Barnard Catalogue of Dark Markings in the Sky (B): 350 dark nebulae
  • Melotte Catalogue of Star Clusters (Mel): 245 star clusters

entry.title: At the End of a Forecast: Revisiting Biology Toward the 21st Century and Its Predictions for 1991–2020
entry.content:
Author: Xiao
Reviewer: Dongda
Night of February 23, 2020

Opening remarks

  This book was jointly edited by the cell biologist Wang Yahui and Chinese Academy of Sciences researcher Wu Zhichun. In the early 1990s, they used questionnaires and expert panels to gather the views of more than 400 specialists in biology-related fields on how the discipline would develop over the next thirty years. The experts considered the broad direction of biology, its likely peaks of development, its major disciplinary questions, and its relationship with other fields. Revisiting the book in 2020 is particularly meaningful. It also explains why biology matters: scientific progress has raised material civilization to great heights, yet cast a deep shadow over spiritual life, even causing spiritual deprivation and collapse. The fundamental way forward, the book argues, is to learn from life itself.

  As everyone knows, “the twenty-first century is the century of biology,” to quote Chen Zhangliang. Biology graduates today face widespread criticism over their job prospects and salaries, but there is no denying that the life sciences, once simply called biology, and biotechnology affect every part of our lives. Consider the recent outbreak: nucleic-acid testing and treatment methods alike depend on advances in biotechnology, while high-throughput testing and drug targeting are themselves subjects of life-science research. This indirectly confirms the value of the forecasts made by senior scholars thirty years ago. Later developments bore out their emphasis on the future importance of molecular biology, brain science and neuroscience, the need to develop behavioral science—mainland China’s first course in the subject had opened at Peking University only in 1988—and the direction of macroecology. The book also proposed a “biopsychosocial medical model,” a concept that seemed ahead of its time to conventional Western medicine but self-evident to traditional Chinese medicine. Two developments, however, went beyond its predictions.

  First, molecular-biology technology advanced far beyond expectations. Reports from the research frontier still focused on determining protein tertiary structures from crystal structures and anticipated further progress along that path, a sound prediction at the time. Those scholars could not have imagined that, more than twenty years later, mature cryo-electron microscopy would make three-dimensional structures more accurate and obtainable for a much wider range of targets. Under Shi Yigong’s leadership, China has also become a world leader in the field. One interesting detail appears in the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ 2013 biological forecast of future scientific development. The volume was divided into sections. Every other article listed several lead authors and collaborating institutions, but the section on the future of structural biology named “Boss Shi” as its sole author, perhaps reflecting the extraordinary caliber of his work. P.S. After attending one of Boss Shi’s classes, a certain Peking University student decided to pursue the life sciences. That says a great deal about Professor Shi’s personal appeal. Sadly, I never had the chance to hear him in person. (A weakling howls from the corner.)

  All right, back to the subject.

  The most intriguing part of the forecast is a section on human functions, including latent functions. It says that the human body possesses extraordinarily refined, flexible, and effective capacities for converting matter and energy, processing information, and regulating itself, capacities many times more sophisticated, flexible, and effective than the artificial functions of machines created by existing science and technology. This, the book argues, shows the importance of studying human functions. What did that phrase mean here? It referred to the meridians and qigong of traditional Chinese medicine, along with the disputed effects of externally emitted qi and paranormal abilities. The book argued that rigorously verifying and scientifically investigating these phenomena and questions would support the healthy development of traditional Chinese medicine. At the time, the field was also called human-body science or human life science. The volume included “A Complementary Understanding of Human Life” by the biomechanics specialist Tao Zulai, who described it as follows: “In human-body science, it is difficult to reconcile its epistemological and methodological foundations with the standards of modern science. It might be called ‘Research into Human Potential and the Functional States of the Movement of Life.’ One may hold that there is a path for understanding the laws governing our own living activity whose epistemological and methodological foundations differ from those of modern science. It is different from, yet complementary to, the cognitive path of the modern life sciences. Chinese medicine represents one system through which humanity understands the movement of its own life. It regards human life as a unity of form (essence), qi, and spirit. Their relationship is: ‘Form is the dwelling place of life; qi is what fills life; spirit is what governs life.’ The meridians are the system through which qi is transported and transformed. The practice of hundreds of millions of people over several thousand years proves that the understanding of human life embodied in Chinese medicine possesses objective, relative truth. Clinical experience tells us that it is impossible to explain the principles of Chinese medicine through modern biomedicine and then regulate Chinese medicine according to modern medicine. This reveals the opposition between the theoretical systems and methodological foundations of Chinese and modern medicine. Only by beginning with their fundamental differences in understanding human life can we establish an internal connection between them and achieve a higher unity. The key is how we understand qi.” Such theories clearly enjoyed considerable acceptance at the time: they appeared in a national outlook on scientific development and occupied substantial space within it. The author also predicted that “qigong medicine will make great strides over the next 10–30 years, establish its own distinctive standards, and achieve relatively wide application.” This truly was the height of the “qigong fever.” Qigong and related theories found their way into many fields. Even Qian Xuesen and other prominent experts published articles on them, and studies appeared claiming that qigong could significantly increase yields in chemical experiments. (I have read several; with my limited knowledge, I could only slap the desk and exclaim, “What extraordinary papers!” Interested readers can search CNKI.) Thirty years later, however, recently published literature shows that academic interest in qigong has clearly waned, while attitudes have reversed completely. It has become closer to entertainment than science. What happened during those thirty years to change the standing of qigong, and of traditional Chinese medicine more broadly, so dramatically? Events in the late 1990s may have dealt qigong a severe blow. But even setting those aside, as students of Chinese medicine, or simply as people with some scientific literacy, we should ask whether the problem lay in the subject itself or in how it developed. How were the experiments in those papers designed? Where were the flaws? If the subject itself was not the problem, how might it continue to develop and flourish? These questions deserve thought and investigation. Attacking Chinese medicine and supporting it uncritically usually arise from the same problem: a single, incomplete perspective. Neither is worth endorsing—or even arguing against.

  Time is the best witness, and no phrase better suits this book. Over thirty years, some disciplines advanced rapidly, while others stood still or gradually declined. What went wrong? Were they unsound from the moment they appeared, or were they simply products of their time? If we believe neither explanation, where does their future lie? Amid the current outbreak, Chinese-medicine treatments have achieved major results and broad recognition from many quarters, proving that our methods are genuinely effective. What, then, can first-year students of Chinese medicine do? The answer is four characters in Chinese: “study hard,” because the best way to repay others is to join the fight ourselves in the future! (I seem to have wandered off topic.) I sincerely hope that Chinese medicine will gain wider recognition and use. At the start of a new decade, may we look back ten years from now and find that it has benefited more people, restored its good name, and opened the way to a better future. It will. The book is certainly old, but it lets us see where biology stood thirty years ago. I have discussed only two examples; much more remains to be discovered in its pages, and many questions still deserve reflection. Let it serve as a reference as we understand the present and look toward the future.

  The book is available in the west-campus library at Beijing University of Chinese Medicine’s Liangxiang campus, so you can borrow it. Alongside our professional studies, we also need to read widely, broaden our horizons, and think carefully. I wonder how everyone has spent the holiday during the outbreak. Online classes have already begun! Pack your little medical-school bags and join me in the ocean of diagnostics, Chinese materia medica, anatomy, histology and embryology, modern Chinese history, ideological and moral cultivation, and English. When studying wears you out, sit down with a book, listen to a song, watch a film, play a game, or jot down the small moments of the day. Each is a fine way to relax. If you have time to spare, why not show off your skills in the kitchen? They say people who can cook are more attractive! Share any of these things, and you might even meet someone whose soul matches your own.

  Finally, finally: enjoy the start of online classes (smile…). I look forward to seeing everyone again at BUCM when spring is warm and the flowers are in bloom, or perhaps in early summer. Washington’s army at Valley Forge will eventually reach Yorktown (that is another story), and we will meet in the place where there is no darkness (the next book!).

entry.title: Fossils in the Milky Way
entry.content:
Author: Kon
Reviewer: Nancy

  Modern cosmology holds that galaxies undergo many mergers as they evolve from their formation to the present day. Their dynamics are too complex for a complete analytical treatment, so researchers generally turn to direct computer simulations of vast numbers of point particles. Astronomy, of course, is ultimately an observational science. Researchers measure the properties of galaxies at different distances—the farther away a galaxy is, the further back in cosmic time we see it, when both the universe and the galaxy were younger—and compare those observations with numerical simulations to determine how well a theoretical model describes reality.

A numerical simulation of the universe's large-scale structure produced by the Max Planck Institute in Germany. The most highly magnified region represents a large galaxy cluster, and each small point of light represents a galaxy.

  Reconstructing the evolutionary history of galaxies has long been an important problem in astronomy. Because we live inside the Milky Way, our own galaxy is an exceptionally valuable object of study, and tracing its history offers an effective test of current theories. Advances in observational technology have now made that work possible, and “galactic archaeology” has become a major field in the era of astronomical big data.

  Galactic archaeology uses the chemical and dynamical properties of stars in the Milky Way to identify unusual structures such as stellar streams and tidal debris. Stars carry a kind of memory. The environments in which old stars formed were very different from their present surroundings, as were the abundances of different heavy elements. Those signatures can still be read in the atmospheres of low-mass stars whose main-sequence lifetimes are especially long. Stars also preserve aspects of their original dynamics. If a group of stars was accreted from another galaxy at some stage in the Milky Way’s history, its motion may differ sharply from that of the Galaxy’s native stars while remaining highly coherent within the group itself. Substructures with distinctive chemical and dynamical signatures can therefore survive as a kind of fossil evidence.

  Astronomers have now found many such substructures within the Milky Way. Some appear to be the remains of globular clusters torn apart by tidal forces; others are traces left by past mergers between the Milky Way and dwarf galaxies.

The spatial distribution of currently known substructures in the Milky Way. Source: arXiv:2002.04340.

entry.title: A Brief History of Humankind: The Sapiens Flood (Part I)
entry.content:
Author: Zikongli

  Today, meet the world’s deadliest animal—No. 1: Homo sapiens. Around 150,000 years ago—or 200,000 years ago, according to some accounts—Homo sapiens began the Cognitive Revolution. They then expanded rapidly from the African grasslands across Eurasia, wiping out most of their fellow species in the genus Homo along the way. Some of those populations’ DNA did manage to hitch a ride on the fast-moving Homo sapiens express. People across Eurasia today generally carry a small amount of Neanderthal DNA.

  For nearly the next hundred thousand years, our Homo sapiens ancestors roamed Eurasia, grinding through the wilderness, spending skill points, and collecting gear. Along the way, they casually eliminated more of their fellow human species, and life was fairly easy. Before long, however, population pressure forced Homo sapiens to begin expanding across the globe. Remember that Homo sapiens had lived in Eurasia for at least 100,000 years after leaving their African homeland. During that time, Eurasia’s other animals coevolved with them. Early Homo sapiens had only recently undergone the Cognitive Revolution and had not yet gained much experience with cooperation and similar skills, giving Eurasian animals time to prepare. They learned to flee when they encountered humans, or to kill a lone human when they found one. (From a carnivore’s perspective, humans are not especially good eating: they are often thin and carry little edible meat.)

  Animals on other continents were not so lucky. Once Homo sapiens had maxed out their experience and equipped themselves with top-tier wilderness gear in Eurasia, they began their first global expansion. About 45,000 years ago, a human tribe set foot on an Australian beach: “Oceania, your emperor has arrived!”

  This was an astonishing step, because even the archipelagos closest to Oceania often contain straits more than 100 kilometers wide. The most plausible theory is that Homo sapiens in the Indonesian archipelago developed a seafaring society and used those skills to overcome one obstacle after another on the way to Oceania. Once there, they felt as though they had entered a new game level. They had never seen species like these: giant kangaroos more than two meters tall, marsupial lions crouching in the grass, enormous lizards, and diprotodons weighing as much as two and a half tons. None of these animals feared humans. After all, humans did not look dangerous. They had neither sharp teeth nor claws, and their bodies were not especially large.

  Even when humans approached, the animals usually ignored them. Homo sapiens exchanged knowing smiles. Of Oceania’s 24 animal species weighing over 50 kilograms, 23 then disappeared… Countless smaller animals vanished as well. Fire mages burned innumerable trees to the ground, leaving only fire-resistant eucalyptus and, of course, the koalas that ate its leaves.

  Homo sapiens were not the sole cause of these extinctions. Climate, the long growth and gestation periods of large animals, and many other factors also played a part. But the MVP was unquestionably Homo sapiens.

entry.title: The Wok's Remarkable History: From Its Origins to the Tang and Song Dynasties
entry.content:
Author: Lai Yuan

The Wok’s Remarkable History (Part I)

  Of all the tools in the kitchen, the wok is king: if it is not frying, it is braising. Three days to master an electric cooker, three years for the ladle, ten years to hone a cleaver, and a lifetime at the iron wok.
Food goes in, wine is poured, and the whole village waits to be served. The fire starts, the spatula rises, and one wok can feed two tables. The dishes arrive, chopsticks are laid out, and friends and family tuck in.
Today, almost every Chinese household has a pitch-black wok. As its Chinese name suggests, its main purpose is stir-frying. Stir-frying is arguably the dominant technique in Chinese cooking today. From ordinary roadside restaurants to five-star hotels, most dishes are prepared either by stir-frying or by some variation on it. The emergence of stir-frying 1,500 years ago laid the foundation for the defining character of later Chinese cuisine, and the technique now satisfies countless hungry diners.

  As the saying goes, “A good wok lasts forever, handed down from one generation to the next.” So just how far back does its history go?

  We must begin with the wok’s elder brother, the iron pot. Both are made of iron, but one came first: the iron pot was the first-generation product, and the wok appeared only after that product was improved and upgraded. It is therefore only fair to call the iron pot the elder brother. Its own history begins with a distant relative, the bronze pot. Bronze vessels were the first metal objects that humans used on a large scale; only after people made bronze pots did the very idea of a pot take shape.

The correct way to use a reconstructed ancient bronze pot

  What? You have never heard of a bronze pot? You must at least recognize a ding. Yes, the ding was the earliest piece of slow-motion-suicide cookware, and it too is a kind of pot.

  Anyone with a basic knowledge of history probably knows that metal goods in the Zhou dynasty were made of bronze. By the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, however, things had changed: anything that could be made of metal was being made of iron.

  So perhaps, during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, people were already hammering out iron versions of the old bronze pots. Even a conservative estimate, then, would place the appearance of the iron pot in that period.

  After all that, let us return to the real subject. As for the wok’s exact date of birth…

  Who knows…

*Qimin Yaoshu* (*Essential Techniques for the Common People*)

  Hey, hey, put down the brick and let us talk this through. I do not know the exact date, but a book from the Northern Wei—commissioned, naturally, by the Northern Wei Publishing House and written by the famous agricultural expert Jia Sixie—contains, somewhere in the Chrysanthemum Treas— sorry, the Qimin Yaoshu, a recipe that has gone down in history, survived to this day, become a household name, earned worldwide fame, and become known to all:

  It is!!!

  scrambledeggs

The Wok’s Remarkable History—Tang: Steam, Boil, Roast; Song: Anything Goes (Part I)

  Last time, we saw that a prototype wok and scrambled eggs cooked in it had already appeared during the Northern and Southern dynasties. Does that mean woks were everywhere by the Tang dynasty?

  History says otherwise. In the Tang, cooking still revolved around the same old trio: steaming, boiling, and roasting.

  The Shuowen Jiezi records: “A ding, with three legs and two handles, is the precious vessel in which the five flavors are blended.”

  It was probably used something like this…⬇

(Surely my concise, crystal-clear drawing has made the correct way to use a *ding* perfectly clear to everyone.)

  The picture makes it obvious that the ding was a tool for boiling and steaming. The method was essentially “throw it all in one big pot”: toss every ingredient in at once, put on the lid, and let it cook.

  ① For one thing, it was extremely convenient. Can you light a fire? Can you add water? Can you put food in? Yes? Then you are done. How convenient is that?

  ② People at the time did not demand much from their food. (You were lucky to have anything to eat; why be picky…?)

  As for whether it tasted good… Sorry, that was outside the scope of consideration.

  But do not look down on steaming and boiling just because the food did not taste good, you dummy. Even today, Western cooks rarely use “steaming.” Take France, whose cuisine is famous worldwide: some say its chefs do not even have a concept of “steaming.”

  Now let us turn to roasting. The Tang campaigns in the north brought large quantities of northern mutton into the empire, along with the soul of barbecue—cumin—from the Middle East. So people in the Tang could enjoy lamb skewers, and lamb was not the only meat they roasted.

Cumin ⬆

  The Tang physician Jiu Yin (who may have spent all day hanging around barbecue stalls) recorded several grilled dishes in the Shiyi Xinjian: mandarin duck, wild boar, eel, myna, and yellow hen.

Be sure to watch to the end!

  Thus, even if the Tang had woks, there was little use for them. They existed, but only in very small numbers. Woks did not begin to become more common until the transition from the Tang to the Song.

  Salt and iron were often state monopolies in imperial China, and the Song was no exception. The government oversaw mining and iron smelting: local mine owners handled extraction, while a “professional team” took care of smelting.

  The “professional team” familiar to us today looks like this:

No explanation needed for this professional team

  The professional iron-smelting team of the time looked like this:

Illustration of wrought- and cast-iron production from *Tiangong Kaiwu*

  That professional team naturally came under the Salt and Iron administration, one of the Northern Song’s Three Financial Bureaus.

(Extra: after the Ming reorganization, during the Yongle reign...)

  The Baoyuan Bureau was originally a mint, the equivalent of a modern coin factory. Ancient currency was made of metal, but everyday pots, bowls, ladles, basins, hoes, rakes, shovels, and the like also required metal. Rather than trouble a second office, the state mint made these farm tools too. Its directors must have found the situation galling: a dignified national mint, reduced to casting farm implements!?

  All right, back to the point. Someone is bound to complain: over the three hundred years between the Tang and Song, were those craftspeople doing nothing but eating? They could not even make something as simple as a wok. Put me in charge and the Tang would be eating stir-fries in minutes. (Doge face.)

  Hey, do not complain that this was slow. A wok “midwife” was nagging away the entire time, pushing for woks to be manufactured and used on a large scale and helping bring the new cooking method called “stir-frying” into the world.

  There was more than one of these busybodies: there were two. One had been chattering without pause from the Han dynasty all the way to the Song, nearly a thousand years. The other began during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

  As for who these two “busybodies” were…

  I will write about that next time…

entry.title: Novel Coronavirus (2019-nCoV)
entry.content:
Author: Shenzhou
Reviewers: DClean and Weiming

  The novel coronavirus outbreak (hereafter 2019-nCoV; online claims that the virus had been named “SARI” were false) has drawn widespread attention across China. As members of the public, whether or not we live in an affected area or have spent time in one, we must remain alert, take proper precautions, and not assume that luck will protect us. We should wear a mask whenever we go out, avoid crowded places wherever possible, and refrain from indoor activities in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces.

Transmission and protection

  Some reports suggest that 2019-nCoV originated in bats or other wild animals, but no official source has confirmed this.

  Because 2019-nCoV is a new virus, anyone who has not previously been infected with the same virus is susceptible, regardless of age. The virus can spread from person to person, most likely through respiratory droplets and contact, with aerosol transmission also a possibility.

  Droplet transmission occurs when a source of infection releases pathogen-bearing secretions and droplets by coughing, sneezing, or speaking, and a susceptible person inhales them. This form of transmission generally requires close contact with the source; beyond two meters, infectiousness largely disappears. It can occur readily in crowded places such as stations, schools, and large gatherings. Contact transmission occurs when a pathogen reaches a susceptible person through direct or indirect contact with a vehicle of transmission. In direct contact transmission, the pathogen passes straight from the source to a suitable portal of entry in the susceptible person. Indirect contact transmission results from touching contaminated objects. Masks provide effective protection against droplet transmission, while rubber gloves can offer some protection against contact transmission.

Symptoms and treatment

  At present, no effective treatment for pneumonia caused by 2019-nCoV has been validated in clinical trials; clinical care consists mainly of symptomatic and supportive treatment. Recent high-throughput drug-screening efforts have identified several drugs that may be effective against 2019-nCoV. Do not blindly trust online rumors or folk remedies. Any unofficial treatment circulated online should be evaluated through scientific reasoning and careful research. Follow official information as it is released to avoid unnecessary problems.

  The main symptoms of pneumonia caused by 2019-nCoV infection are fever, cough, and fatigue, and more than half of patients experience difficulty breathing. Some people may not develop a fever. It is also worth noting that patients infected with 2019-nCoV rarely show upper-respiratory symptoms, such as a runny nose, sneezing, or a sore throat, or intestinal symptoms.

  Sneezing is a response to irritation of the nasal mucosa, and much of the expelled air leaves through the nose. Coughing, by contrast, is a response to irritation of the trachea, bronchial mucosa, or pleura, and the expelled air leaves mainly through the mouth. The two should be distinguished. If upper-respiratory symptoms appear, an upper-respiratory infection rather than the novel pneumonia should be considered.

  Patients with similar symptoms that are not severe—a temperature below 38°C and no difficulty breathing—should first call a nearby community doctor. Wearing full protective equipment, the doctor can visit the home and determine whether a trip to a designated hospital is necessary, reducing the risk of cross-infection while seeking care. Patients with severe symptoms should immediately call the local designated hospital and center for disease control and prevention, then put on the recommended protection and go to the hospital as instructed.

entry.title: Do We Get Overtime Pay in a Leap Year?
entry.content:
Author: Saito Shin
Reviewer: Baiyan

  If my math is right, this article will be put on public display for your judgment on Lunar New Year’s Day (or sometime afterward). Happy New Year, everyone! Posting on New Year’s Day is no easy task. I’m not asking for triple pay (or any pay at all); all I ask is that you give it a careful read. If you could give it the usual like-comment-favorite combo (scratch that) and share it, even better!

Wishing everyone a happy, healthy New Year!

  You have probably heard that 2020 is a “double leap year.” The Year of the Rat has 384 days, which means an extra month of work thanks to the leap fourth lunar month. The math makes sense, but why should we have to work overtime? Today, let us take a look at intercalation in calendars.

  First, what exactly is a “calendar”?

  A calendar is a system for determining the lengths of days, months, and years and the relationships among them. In other words, it sets the order by which we measure time. Some calendar months and years take their lengths from the cycles of the Sun and Moon; others are fixed by convention. The earliest calendars paid close attention to the Moon’s waxing and waning. Later, agriculture made it important for calendars to keep the seasons regular and seasonal markers in the proper order. These rules kept the sequence of months and days aligned with the apparent positions of the Sun and Moon in the sky. Without that alignment, the seasons would eventually be turned upside down and lunar phases would fall out of step.

  Next, what is “intercalation”?

  The tropical year measures the cycle of the seasons, while the synodic month measures the cycle of the lunar phases. Calendar makers therefore need an accurate length for each. Yet neither the tropical year (365.2422 days) nor the synodic month (29.5306 days) contains a whole number of days, and the two periods are not simply commensurable. If a calendar used their exact astronomical lengths, years and months would begin at a different time of day on each cycle (and how are we supposed to spend 0.2422 of a day?). That would be highly inconvenient for work and daily life. Calendars instead assign whole numbers of days to their years and months, creating what are called calendar years and calendar months. This leaves discrepancies between the calendar and the astronomical periods. Left uncorrected, those discrepancies build up and eventually throw the calendar into disorder. Correcting for them is what calendar makers call intercalation.

  Most readers already know how intercalation works in the Gregorian calendar, the solar calendar now in common use. A solar calendar takes the tropical year as its basic unit and does not follow the synodic month. It treats the year as the primary unit and aims to keep the mean calendar year equal to the tropical year; the number of days in each month and the number of months in each year are set by convention. Today’s worldwide civil calendar developed from the Julian calendar. The Julian calendar assigned 365.25 days to a tropical year and twelve months to each year. Odd-numbered months had 31 days; even-numbered months had 30, except February, which had 29 because it was then the month in which prisoners were executed. A leap day was added to February after every three ordinary years, bringing it to 30 days in a leap year. Later misunderstandings resulted in twelve leap years over a span of 33 years, three more than intended. The ruler at the time ordered two corrections. First, leap years would be suspended for the next eleven years; once the three extra leap years had been offset, the four-year cycle would resume. Second, August, his birth month, would become a long month. The pattern of long and short months after August was reversed, and the extra day was taken from February. February consequently has 28 days in an ordinary year and 29 in a leap year.

  The Julian calendar was arguably the best calendar of its time. Several Christian countries in Europe agreed to adopt it and, based on the astronomical observations then available, fixed the vernal equinox on March 21. The Julian year, however, is 0.0078 day longer than the tropical year. Over 1,257 years, that small difference added up to an error of about ten days, so that by 1582 the Sun was observed to cross the vernal equinox on March 11. Pope Gregory XIII accepted a proposal by the Italian physician and philosopher Lilio and decreed two changes: the ten days from October 5 through October 14 that year would be dropped, and the rule of one leap year every four years would be replaced with 97 leap years every 400 years. The new rule is the one we know today. A year divisible by 100 is a century leap year only if it is also divisible by 400; every other year divisible by 4 is a leap year. The reformed calendar became known as the Gregorian calendar. It is far more accurate than the Julian calendar, although it still gains 1.2 days in 4,000 years. The years 4000 and 8000 should therefore not be leap years (unless a better calendar has been devised by then).

  To understand intercalation in the traditional Chinese calendar, we first need to know how that calendar is constructed. It is lunisolar, not purely lunar as it is often said to be. A lunar calendar makes the month its primary unit and sets the length of a calendar month by the synodic month. The length of its calendar year is fixed by convention and has no relation to the tropical year. A synodic month lasts 29.5306 days. Lunar calendars therefore give 30 days to odd-numbered months and 29 days to even-numbered months, beginning each month with the first appearance of the new Moon. Twelve months make a 354-day year. Twelve synodic months, however, total 354.3671 days, so over thirty years they exceed thirty calendar years by 11.013 days. Such a calendar stays in step with the phases of the Moon, but each ordinary year is about eleven days shorter than the tropical year. It falls behind by a month in three years, and after about seventeen years the order of its months and seasons would be reversed. That would make it a poor guide to agriculture. The traditional Chinese calendar was developed to resolve this conflict.

  A lunisolar calendar gives equal weight to the year and the month. It uses the synodic month as the length of a calendar month, then inserts leap months to keep the calendar year aligned with the tropical year. The tropical year contains about 12.368 synodic months. To keep the average calendar year close to the tropical year, an ordinary lunisolar year has twelve months and a leap year has thirteen. The additional month is the leap month. Calculations show that seven leap months in nineteen years is a reasonable arrangement, one that keeps the order of the months from drifting away from the seasons. Inserting leap months creates a large difference in year length: an ordinary year has 353 to 355 days, while a leap year has 383 to 384. So yes, you really do get another month’s salary; there is no need to feel cheated. The placement of the leap month is closely tied to the twelve principal terms among the twenty-four solar terms. Strictly speaking, the system comprises twelve principal terms and twelve sectional terms. In a lunisolar calendar, every month normally contains a designated principal term, a detail we will leave aside here. Nineteen tropical years contain 228 sectional terms and 228 principal terms, while nineteen lunisolar years contain 235 synodic months. Seven months must therefore lack a sectional term, and seven must lack a principal term. Under the rule eventually adopted, a month without a principal term becomes that year’s leap month. It takes the name of the preceding month with the word “leap” placed before it. Calendar makers have followed this method ever since.

  Why, then, do we never seem to encounter a leap first lunar month? Earth passes aphelion in early July each year, roughly around the beginning of the sixth lunar month. At that point, Earth is moving more slowly along its orbit, while successive principal terms remain 30° apart in the Sun’s apparent ecliptic longitude. The interval between them is therefore longer, making a leap month more likely. As far as I know, no leap first lunar month will occur between now and 2060. Until then, a two-month winter vacation is out of the question.

entry.title: Tumors Explained
entry.content:
Author: 绿水青山
Reviewers: 食野; 未名

  Most of us have encountered the word “tumor” in everyday life without necessarily knowing its technical definition. The word often inspires immediate fear. Malignant tumors are generally difficult to cure and can have an enormous effect on a patient’s daily life. Here, we will look at some basic facts about tumors.

  In biology, a tumor is a neoplasm formed by the abnormal proliferation of the body’s cells—in other words, a mass produced by the abnormal growth of body tissue. It commonly appears as a localized mass of abnormal tissue. Tumors form when various tumor-causing factors severely disrupt the regulation of cell growth.

  This definition tells us that a tumor should not exist when the body is functioning normally. What, then, characterizes neoplastic proliferation? First, it is uncoordinated with the body and harmful to it. It is also generally clonal, and tumor cells lose their ability to differentiate and mature to varying degrees. Their original function, morphology, and metabolism usually become abnormal. At the same time, they grow vigorously, escape control, and acquire a degree of autonomy. Early in tumor formation, an external carcinogenic factor alters a cell’s genes. The cell escapes control and can reliably pass those altered genes to the next generation. Even if the external factor is later removed, the tumor continues to proliferate on its own. A tumor is generally composed of daughter cells descended from the same original cell.

  With the features of neoplastic proliferation in mind, we can turn to the usual morphology of tumors. A tumor mass is most often solitary, although several may appear at once. Tumors take many shapes, including polypoid, papillary, cauliflower-like, nodular, and ulcerative forms. Their colors vary as well. A cut surface is generally gray-white or gray-red, although its color also depends on blood content, pigments, and other factors. Lipomas, for example, are usually yellow, whereas hemangiomas are often dark red or purplish red. Tumors can also be classified as benign or malignant according to their growth. Medical naming conventions differ between the two. A malignant epithelial tumor is generally named for its “primary site” followed by “carcinoma,” whereas a benign tumor is named for its “location” followed by “tumor” or “-oma.” There are exceptions: a malignant tumor arising in mesenchymal tissue, for example, is called a “sarcoma.”

I. Benign tumors

  One clear distinction between benign and malignant tumors is the way they grow. A benign tumor expands in place and does not spread to other parts of the body. A malignant tumor grows invasively and may metastasize from its primary organ to other sites. At the cellular level, benign tumors show relatively few atypical mitotic figures and grow more slowly. A benign tumor generally remains in a single location and is usually enclosed by a fibrous capsule. It therefore tends to cause less harm, with damage generally limited to local compression or obstruction. Treatment is comparatively straightforward. Most benign tumors have a good prognosis and do not readily recur.

II. Malignant tumors (cancer)

  Malignant tumors are generally called cancer. Because they grow invasively, they can seriously affect surrounding tissues, spreading through them much like tree roots. Atypical mitotic figures are common in malignant tumor cells. During metastasis, genetic changes also alter the cells’ adhesion, motility, and ability to degrade the extracellular matrix, allowing them to break through the basement membrane and invade surrounding tissue. If they then enter blood or lymphatic vessels, leave those vessels at a suitable point, and continue proliferating elsewhere, the tumor has metastasized. This is a principal reason malignant tumors threaten patients’ lives. Besides causing greater harm, malignant tumors require more complex treatment, and the outcome is generally less satisfactory.

  The growth rate of tumor cells is generally affected by the following factors:

  1. The doubling time of the tumor cells;
  2. The growth fraction—the proportion of cells in the population that are proliferating;
  3. The production and loss of tumor cells;

  Research has found that the doubling time of cells in most malignant tumors is similar to, or even longer than, that of normal cells. The rapid growth of malignant tumors therefore does not come from a shorter doubling time. The latter two factors have a greater effect on their growth rate.

  The distinction between benign and malignant is not absolute; it is a boundary drawn by people. Some tumors have tissue morphology and biological behavior that fall between the two. Such tumors generally tend toward malignant transformation or display some features of malignancy. An ovarian borderline serous tumor, for example, lies between benign and malignant. Some benign tumors may also become malignant if they are not treated promptly. In exceptionally rare cases, a malignant tumor may stop growing or even regress spontaneously for reasons such as stronger immune function.

entry.title: The Feathered Sprites on My Campus
entry.content:
Author: 蜗牛
Reviewer: 一毫秒的永恒

  A winter morning is cold and still. The sun has not yet cast its highlights across the world, so everything retains its natural color. I love this hour: no noise, no distractions, no rush before first period. I can leave home at an easy pace, clock in, and bring my binoculars along to watch the birds on campus.

  The day is off to a good start. Soon after leaving home, amid the magpie calls in the little square by the water tower, I pick out a faint zi-zi from the sparrows’ chatter. Probably a tit. Through my binoculars, it looks like a great tit, though it might be a Japanese tit. I confuse the two every time. Even familiar birds make me look closely.

  Beyond the small central gate, the plane-tree avenue between the sports field and the shops is a veritable “path of angels”—or, more accurately, angel droppings. Broad patches of bird mess merge across the pavement. Perhaps the birds meet here every day. Around the turn from spring to summer, many people on this road have been challenged by azure-winged magpies. First, a large bird appears on a low branch off to one side and lets loose a scolding barrage. The moment you pass its perch, a gust brushes the back of your head. By the time you turn around, the magpie has declared victory and retreated. It never quite attacks; it merely circles extremely close behind and above your head once you pass. I have no idea what kind of tactic that is. Once, I kept my head turned and watched the bird deliver its warning. Under my stare, it seemed too embarrassed to make a move. I eventually backed out of its territory, privately delighted for some time by the helpless look in its eyes.

Eurasian magpie

  Real attacks do happen, though rarely. A close friend told me that she was playing with her son on this road when a young azure-winged magpie fluttered nearby. The two- or three-year-old ventured a little too close, and an adult bird dived at him. She rushed forward to shield the child. A day later, walking the same stretch without her son, she was swooped from behind by the adult, which pecked the top of her head. It truly hurt. She was wearing different clothes, so how had the bird recognized her? To us, birds of the same species and size can be nearly impossible to tell apart. I do not know whether the bird I meet on the road is the same one I see outside my window. How, then, can a bird single out the same person in different clothes from a crowd?

Spotted dove

  Even on this avenue ruled by azure-winged magpies, a dove will occasionally hide in silence. Whenever I spot one, my eyes go straight to its collar. So far, campus has shown me spotted doves in black-and-white pearl necklaces, but never an Oriental turtle dove with a striped black-and-white collar. I will keep checking every dove I meet.

  After twenty-two years on this campus, I know every tree and every blade of grass. A tree at the southwest corner of the sports field became our “king of trees” thanks to a leaking underground pipe. The same leak later led to its crown being cut off. But a king remains a king: the tree poured all its stored strength into the largest leaves we had ever seen and once again became the center of attention. Here, too, I once encountered a grey-headed woodpecker and a flock of white-cheeked starlings stopping on their southward migration.

  Along Magnolia Avenue, red-billed blue magpies and light-vented bulbuls greet me cheerfully from the magnolias or the cedars in the rose garden. I know where they are headed. The bulbuls will sing from the pines south of the western classroom building. The blue magpies will furtively rummage through the trash can beside the western wall. Do they not know about the one by the northeastern wall, or have the crows claimed it?

  After clocking in at the office building, I can stroll over to the little garden in front of the western classroom building and try my luck. In the morning, that garden is luckier than the one in front of the eastern building; in the afternoon, the reverse is true. After some thought, I decided sunlight must be the reason. A row of tall cedars stands along the gardens’ southern edge, with the school wall behind it. In the morning, the trees keep every ray of sunlight out of the eastern garden, while sunshine reaches straight across from the office square to the western one. Here I have watched yellow-bellied tits hopping through willow branches. Here, too, students and I have quietly watched a crowned hoopoe on a winter morning, cold and still, before the sun had cast its highlights across the world and while everything retained its natural color—the hour I love, free of noise, distraction, and the rush before first period, when I can leave home at an easy pace, clock in, and bring my binoculars to watch campus birds. Even when luck offers nothing else, the light-vented bulbuls singing at full voice from the cedar tops never disappoint. Their calls at this hour vary endlessly and never become tiresome. From the little garden, I continue west to the wall and then turn north. Soon I will see my favorite sprite. The thought brings a little anticipation and a little excitement.

Daurian redstart

  First comes the Daurian redstart, a milestone in my life as a birdwatcher. Because of this little creature, I searched Baidu for two years and accidentally joined a QQ group for bird sellers before finally finding the “Chinese Birdwatchers” group. These days, I no longer search everywhere for the redstart’s hiding place. Its thin, crisp, metallic di is enough to make me picture it bobbing its head and flicking its tail. In that respect, it resembles the wagtails that often work out on the sports field.

Black-throated bushtit

  The other is the black-throated bushtit, affectionately known as the “little redhead.” Spotting one of China’s smallest birds takes both patience and luck. I usually listen first for a very soft zi-zi. With experience, a faint sound nearby becomes distinguishable from a loud one far away. I stand still and watch. When something flickers among the branches, I raise my binoculars, and the little bird appears: a narrow white line around its neck above a black, diamond-shaped patch. Then I check the forehead. If the crown is chestnut-red rather than pure black, it is my little redhead. Only when my arms and back ache from holding the binoculars so long do I lower them and walk away content. Beside a bushtit scarcely visible to the naked eye, a large red-billed blue magpie makes the scene feel perfectly peaceful.

Chinese blackbird

  Farther on is the western dining hall, an excellent spot. Birds can eat, drink, play, brawl, and argue there, with only a wall separating them from the grove outside the school. It offers both an outpost and an escape route, so it is no surprise that black drongos make it their early-summer base. I still wonder whether the great spotted woodpecker fills its stomach in the trees or on the ground in front of the dining hall. Two winters ago, a flock of light-vented bulbuls quarreled with a blackbird here so loudly that I heard them from twenty meters away. Unable to see the blackbird at first, I assumed an azure-winged magpie had upset the bulbuls. The magpies had nothing to do with it; only then did I spot the blackbird. I saw no blackbirds for the rest of that winter or the next, and thought they had left campus for good. Then, all at once, there they were before me: one, two, five—no, more still—a whole flock of at least seven or eight. At the sight of me, they scattered from a tree in the flower bed to the great cedar by the dining-hall entrance, over the wall a few meters away, then back again to hide among the privet leaves. One greedy bird on the ground refused to leave. Its orange-yellow bill gave it an endearingly foolish look. Standing still, it held its head high and alert. The moment it began walking, its anxiety showed: head down and thrust forward, a few hurried steps, then a halt with head raised, then neck out and head down for another quick dash. The pattern repeated until I was laughing to myself. Compared with a magpie’s calm, unhurried stride, it made me spare a moment’s sympathy for the pressures these birds face.

Eurasian tree sparrow

  This beautiful campus has been my home. Now I am about to leave the place where I have lived and worked for twenty-two years, and I am deeply reluctant to go. I remember the pagoda tree between the dormitories, with its flat hornet’s nest shaped like a sesame cake. I remember Oriental greenfinches calling from the crowns of white poplars. But do they remember me—the person who, before learning the ethics of birdwatching, once frightened apart a mixed flock of sparrows and greenfinches feeding on the sports field, simply to tell more quickly which bird belonged to which species?

The author’s school: Mianchi High School, Henan

entry.title: From Simple to Complex: Algebra, Part 1
entry.content:
Algebra is the branch of mathematics concerned with numbers, quantities, relationships, structures, and general methods for solving algebraic equations and systems. Elementary algebra, usually taught in secondary school, introduces the basic ideas: how addition and multiplication behave, what variables are, and how to construct polynomials and find their roots. The subject reaches far beyond numbers to encompass all kinds of abstract structures.

  Author: delta

  Algebra is one of the central branches of modern mathematics. It divides into many subjects of its own, from elementary algebra to higher algebra, which branches still further. If mathematics is Yggdrasil, then algebra is Asgard.

  Geometry is Vanaheim.

  Within this Asgard, abstract algebra plainly wields the same authority that Odin commands in Valhalla. Our goal is to seek an audience with him. But no kingdom lets a traveler walk straight up to its king without first passing the gatekeeper. So let us step onto Bifrost and have a heart-to-heart with Heimdall, who plays the part of elementary algebra.

Origins

  Diophantus, a Greek mathematician of the third century CE, is widely regarded as the father of algebra, while al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician of the medieval Arab world, is credited with founding the subject itself. Chinese students often make fun of al-Khwarizmi because of how his name sounds in Chinese.

  That ill-judged teasing has not exactly made al-Khwarizmi famous. Only a small minority have heard of him. Diophantus, by contrast, is widely known for the elementary math-contest puzzle on his tombstone and for Diophantine equations.

  Here the story takes another amusing turn: many people have heard of Diophantine equations, but not only can they not solve one, they do not even know what one is.

  If you think this article is about to explain Diophantine equations, think again. We promised to work from the simple to the complex, and a Diophantine equation is not nearly simple enough. Its essence, however, is.

  What is the essence of an equation? An equality.

  What lies at the heart of an equality? “={=}=”.

  Let us begin with the equals sign and descend into Mímir’s well.

The Equals Sign

  To begin, we know that the following statements are true:

1=12=1+12×5−6=2×2\begin{aligned}1 &= 1 \\2 &= 1 + 1 \\2 \times 5 - 6 &= 2 \times 2\end{aligned}122×5−6​=1=1+1=2×2​

  Why are they true? Because Odin’s divine authority says so. We will have to wait for our audience with him to ask why. For now, the point is simply that we all recognize these statements as true.

  But we could replace the numbers on either side of these equalities in infinitely many ways. Our time is limited, and video games are always calling, so we need a way to talk about numbers in general. Since the job begins by finding substitutes for specific numbers, we shall call it the “algebra project.”

  That gives us the following equalities, which are also plainly true:

x=x(a+b)x=ax+bx(a−b)x=ax−bx\begin{aligned}x &= x \\(a + b)x &= ax + bx \\(a - b)x &= ax - bx\end{aligned}x(a+b)x(a−b)x​=x=ax+bx=ax−bx​

  (Odin, speaking from behind the scenes: In fact, this is because (R−{0},+,⋅)(R - \{0\}, +, \cdot)(R−{0},+,⋅) is a commutative ring. Never mind my circular definition.)

  For the real numbers and the four basic arithmetic operations, these equalities follow from the “Thrud-commutative law,” the “Hildr-associative law,” and the “Olrun-distributive law.” Heimdall taught you how to use those operations and laws.

  What? You have forgotten who Heimdall is? He is elementary algebra in this story. Keep up!

  (Heimdall: You have hurt my feelings. Sniff.)

  Since you forgot him, Heimdall wants revenge. Asgard is a civilized realm, however, so his revenge takes a civilized form: a set of problems. Fail to solve them, and you will never reach Asgard.

  Heimdall’s question 1: Prove that (a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2(a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2.

  Too easy. With help from the Valkyries, you solve it in no time.

(a+b)2=(a+b)(a+b)=a(a+b)+b(a+b)=a2+ab+ba+b2=a2+ab+ab+b2=a2+2ab+b2.\begin{aligned}(a + b)^2 &= (a + b)(a + b) \\&= a(a + b) + b(a + b) \\&= a^2 + ab + ba + b^2 \\&= a^2 + ab + ab + b^2 \\&= a^2 + 2ab + b^2.\end{aligned}(a+b)2​=(a+b)(a+b)=a(a+b)+b(a+b)=a2+ab+ba+b2=a2+ab+ab+b2=a2+2ab+b2.​

  Heimdall refuses to give in and sets you another problem.

  Heimdall’s question 2: Prove that (a+b+e)2=a2+b2+e2+2ab+2be+2ca(a + b + e)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + e^2 + 2ab + 2be + 2ca(a+b+e)2=a2+b2+e2+2ab+2be+2ca.

  This one has an extra quantity and is therefore a little more complicated, but the Valkyries help you through it.

Immediate, obvious, and trivial; proceed as in the previous example. Left as an exercise. Solution omitted. The proof is straightforward.
The converse is similar, and the corollary follows. Details omitted. QED. Thus proved.

  Just as Heimdall is reluctantly preparing to let you pass, you cannot resist asking, “Who are these three goddesses beside me, the ones calling themselves Valkyries and helping me all this time?”

  The three Valkyries, the “Thrud-commutative law,” the “Hildr-associative law,” and the “Olrun-distributive law,” are furious that you have never read any Norse mythology (mathematics). They promptly detain you. While you are wondering how to escape, Heimdall offers a hand.

  There is no such thing as a free lunch, of course. First, you must help Heimdall with a problem.

  Heimdall’s question 3: Prove that (∑i=1nai)2=∑i=1nai2+2∑1≤i<j≤naiaj.\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 + 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} a_i a_j.(∑i=1n​ai​)2=∑i=1n​ai2​+2∑1≤i<j≤n​ai​aj​.

  You have two choices: admit that you do not know what ∑\sum∑ means, or prove the result.

  Then it comes back to you:

∑i=1nai=a1+a2+Λ+an.∑1≤i<j≤naiaj=a1a2+a1a3+Λ+a1an+a2a3+a2a4+Λ+a2an+Λ+an−1an.\begin{aligned}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i &= a_1 + a_2 + \Lambda + a_n. \\[0.9em]\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} a_i a_j &= a_1 a_2 + a_1 a_3 + \Lambda + a_1 a_n \\[0.9em]&+ a_2 a_3 + a_2 a_4 + \Lambda + a_2 a_n \\[0.9em]&+ \Lambda \\[0.9em]&+ a_{n-1} a_n.\end{aligned}i=1∑n​ai​1≤i<j≤n∑​ai​aj​​=a1​+a2​+Λ+an​.=a1​a2​+a1​a3​+Λ+a1​an​+a2​a3​+a2​a4​+Λ+a2​an​+Λ+an−1​an​.​

  That leaves only the second option. But how do you expand the square of a sum with nnn terms?

  Suddenly, you remember again: mathematical induction.

    First prove the statement for n=1n = 1n=1;

    then assume it holds for n=mn = mn=m and show that it must also hold for n=m+1n = m + 1n=m+1.

    The equality plainly holds for n=1,2,3n = 1,2,3n=1,2,3. Now:

    Assume the statement holds for n=mn = mn=m. For n=m+1n = m + 1n=m+1:

(∑i=1m+1ai)2=(∑i=1mai+am+1)2=(∑i=1mai)2+2∑i=1maiam+1+am+12=∑i=1mai2+2∑1≤i<j≤maiaj+2∑i=1maiam+1+am+12=∑i=1m+1ai2+2∑1≤i<j≤m+1aiaj.\begin{aligned}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m+1} a_i\right)^2 &= \left(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i + a_{m+1}\right)^2 \\[0.9em]&= \left(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\right)^2 + 2 \sum_{i=1}^m a_i a_{m+1} + a_{m+1}^2 \\[0.9em]&= \sum_{i=1}^m a_i^2 + 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le m} a_i a_j + 2 \sum_{i=1}^m a_i a_{m+1} + a_{m+1}^2 \\[0.9em]&= \sum_{i=1}^{m+1} a_i^2 + 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le m+1} a_i a_j.\end{aligned}(i=1∑m+1​ai​)2​=(i=1∑m​ai​+am+1​)2=(i=1∑m​ai​)2+2i=1∑m​ai​am+1​+am+12​=i=1∑m​ai2​+21≤i<j≤m∑​ai​aj​+2i=1∑m​ai​am+1​+am+12​=i=1∑m+1​ai2​+21≤i<j≤m+1∑​ai​aj​.​

  Heimdall is pleased, but not satisfied:

  Heimdall’s question 4: Prove that ∑1≤i<j≤n(ai−aj)2=n∑i=1nai2−(∑i=1nai)2.\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} (a_i - a_j)^2 = n \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2.∑1≤i<j≤n​(ai​−aj​)2=n∑i=1n​ai2​−(∑i=1n​ai​)2.

  This time, we need to count how often each aaa appears, so you search your memory once more.

  You suddenly remember, for the third time now (that protagonist’s plot armor is getting rather strong): the Fubini principle.

  Also known as double counting, the principle proves an equality by calculating the same quantity in two different ways. It extends to the evaluation of multiple integrals but is also a standard tool in combinatorics.

  For a2a^2a2, the cases j=2,3,Λ,nj = 2,3,\Lambda,nj=2,3,Λ,n produce a total of n−1n - 1n−1 occurrences;

  For aaa, the cases j=3,4,Λ,nj = 3,4,\Lambda,nj=3,4,Λ,n produce n−2n - 2n−2 occurrences, and the case i=1i = 1i=1, j=2j = 2j=2 supplies one more, for n−1n-1n−1 in all;

  by the same reasoning, every aia_iai​ occurs n−1n-1n−1 times. Therefore:

∑1≤i<j≤n(ai−aj)2=(n−1)∑i=1nai2−2∑1≤i<j≤naiaj=n∑i=1nai2−(∑i=1nai)2.\begin{aligned}\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} (a_i - a_j)^2 &= (n-1) \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 - 2 \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} a_i a_j \\[0.9em]&= n \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 - \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^2.\end{aligned}1≤i<j≤n∑​(ai​−aj​)2​=(n−1)i=1∑n​ai2​−21≤i<j≤n∑​ai​aj​=ni=1∑n​ai2​−(i=1∑n​ai​)2.​

  Counting terms this way is remarkably convenient, and you glide through the next problem:

  Heimdall’s question 5: Prove that (∑i=1nai)(∑j=1nbj)=12∑i=1n∑j=1n(aibj+ajbi).\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right) \left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\right) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n (a_i b_j + a_j b_i).(∑i=1n​ai​)(∑j=1n​bj​)=21​∑i=1n​∑j=1n​(ai​bj​+aj​bi​).

  For each fixed aia_iai​, every bjb_jbj​ enters the expansion. Across the nnn choices of the other index, the same relabeling works for each fixed bjb_jbj​. Therefore:

(∑i=1nai)(∑j=1nbj)=∑i=1n∑j=1naibj=∑i=1n∑j=1najbi=12∑i=1n∑j=1n(aibj+ajbi).\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right) \left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_i b_j = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_j b_i = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n (a_i b_j + a_j b_i).(i=1∑n​ai​)(j=1∑n​bj​)=i=1∑n​j=1∑n​ai​bj​=i=1∑n​j=1∑n​aj​bi​=21​i=1∑n​j=1∑n​(ai​bj​+aj​bi​).

  As the saying goes, three strikes ought to be enough. No one knows whether Asgard has the same proverb, but perhaps Qin Shi Huang’s planet-destroying warships carried it from the Chinese Lostbelt all the way to Northern Europe. Heimdall agrees to rescue you.

  The moment you step out of the cell, however, you run into the three Valkyries.

  Oh no—the Three Pillars.

  Rather than break his oath, Heimdall goes to war with the Valkyries. According to Lu Xun’s classic theory that “the North always wins a civil war” (Lu Xun: I never said that), Heimdall, who serves the Northern Empire, ultimately prevails. That is a story from another world, perhaps from a certain Tencent game. Plenty of examples seem to support the theory, including the American Civil War.

  The Valkyries agree to let Heimdall take you away, but only if you solve one more problem:

  Valkyrie’s question: Prove that (∑i=1nai2)(∑i=1nbi2)≥(∑i=1naibi)2\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \right)\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^2 \right) \ge \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \right)^2(∑i=1n​ai2​)(∑i=1n​bi2​)≥(∑i=1n​ai​bi​)2

  You know this one! It is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, jokingly nicknamed “Cauchy washes socks” in Chinese.

  Wait. An inequality? Weren’t we talking about equalities? Where did this come from?

  (Odin, speaking from behind the scenes: Inequalities arise from equalities.)

  Oh. Right. From equalities.

  Odin has given you a hint. You stop and think.

  For the fourth time, something suddenly comes back to you: Lagrange’s identity. After all that practice with Heimdall, you quickly obtain:

(∑i=1nai2)(∑i=1nbi2)−(∑i=1naibi)2=∑i=1n∑j=1nai2bj2−∑i=1n∑j=1naibiajbj=12∑i=1n∑j=1n(ai2bj2+aj2bi2−2aibiajbj)=12∑i=1n∑j=1n(aibj−ajbi)2=∑1≤i<j≤n(aibj−ajbi)2≥0.\begin{aligned}\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \right)\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i^2 \right) - \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \right)^2&= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_i^2 b_j^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_i b_i a_j b_j \\[0.9em]&= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \left( a_i^2 b_j^2 + a_j^2 b_i^2 - 2a_i b_i a_j b_j \right) \\[0.9em]&= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \left( a_i b_j - a_j b_i \right)^2 \\[0.9em]&= \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} \left( a_i b_j - a_j b_i \right)^2 \ge 0.\end{aligned}(i=1∑n​ai2​)(i=1∑n​bi2​)−(i=1∑n​ai​bi​)2​=i=1∑n​j=1∑n​ai2​bj2​−i=1∑n​j=1∑n​ai​bi​aj​bj​=21​i=1∑n​j=1∑n​(ai2​bj2​+aj2​bi2​−2ai​bi​aj​bj​)=21​i=1∑n​j=1∑n​(ai​bj​−aj​bi​)2=1≤i<j≤n∑​(ai​bj​−aj​bi​)2≥0.​

  Remove the final “greater than or equal to zero,” and the calculation is a proof of Lagrange’s identity. So inequalities really can emerge from equalities.

  The inequalities between means can likewise be proved from an equality. The argument is too involved for this article, but readers can find it in Chen Ji’s Algebraic Inequalities.

  To keep you from being detained again, Heimdall teaches you a few more tales from Norse mythology (mathematics):

  Abel transformation:

∑k=mnfk(gk+1−gk)=[fn+1gn+1−fmgm]−∑k=mngk+1(fk+1−fk)\sum_{k=m}^{n} f_k \left( g_{k+1} - g_k \right) = \left[ f_{n+1} g_{n+1} - f_m g_m \right] - \sum_{k=m}^{n} g_{k+1} \left( f_{k+1} - f_k \right)k=m∑n​fk​(gk+1​−gk​)=[fn+1​gn+1​−fm​gm​]−k=m∑n​gk+1​(fk+1​−fk​)

  where {fk}\{f_k\}{fk​} and {gk}\{g_k\}{gk​} are any two sequences.

  Schur’s inequality:

a,b,c>0, r∈R  ⟹  ar(a−b)(a−c)+br(b−c)(b−a)+cr(c−a)(c−b)≥0a,b,c>0,\ r\in\mathbb{R} \implies a^r(a-b)(a-c) + b^r(b-c)(b-a) + c^r(c-a)(c-b) \ge 0a,b,c>0, r∈R⟹ar(a−b)(a−c)+br(b−c)(b−a)+cr(c−a)(c−b)≥0

  This, too, can be proved with an equality. The proof is left to the reader.

  At last, Heimdall leads you across Bifrost, the rainbow bridge. You have taken your first real step toward an audience with Odin. Little do you know that Thor, Sif, and the trickster Loki are waiting ahead…

entry.title: A Brief History of Humankind: The Cognitive Revolution
entry.content:
Author: 自控力
Reviewer: Nancy

  The familiar “march of human evolution” is misleading. Human evolution was not the straight, single-track road shown in that image, but a flourishing tree with many branches. More than fifteen known species once belonged to the genus Homo. Neanderthals, Homo erectus, Homo floresiensis, and others shared the Earth with our ancestors, Homo sapiens, for long stretches of time.

  Where did this deeply misleading linear image come from? It first appeared in the popular-science book Early Man, published in 1965. The book originally included an elegant, elongated foldout depicting hominins at different stages. Because the illustration was so long, later layouts compressed and folded it to save space. The figures consequently appeared to be walking forward in a line, eventually giving us the linear version familiar today.

  In the struggle for survival on ancient Earth, Homo sapiens was not as strong as the Neanderthals, nor were we the most agile. Why, over the long course of time, did all our other “brothers and sisters” become extinct, while only we

  Researchers studying human origins generally agree that modern Homo sapiens arose in sub-Saharan Africa, centered on the East African Rift, where our ancestors gradually emerged several million years ago. Some fossils, however, suggest that members of the genus Homo may also have lived elsewhere in the world during the same period. This evidence has given rise to two principal frameworks: the Out-of-Africa hypothesis and the multiregional hypothesis.

  Early human groups did not differ greatly from one another. Many left Africa and evolved separately in different regions, gradually becoming distinct archaic human populations. The process resembled the branching of the cat family into lions, tigers, leopards, and other very different animals. Among the human species that evolved early were the robust Neanderthals and the diminutive Homo floresiensis. All had learned to think, but the expansion of the brain came at a heavy cost for early humans.

  A mammal weighing about 60 kilograms generally has a brain volume of roughly 200 cubic centimeters, whereas early humans such as Homo habilis already had brains of about 600 cubic centimeters. It was as though they had installed an extra, high-performance CPU. Humans then relied on their exceptional intelligence and struggled onward for tens of thousands of years, until at last… nothing happened. At first, a more capable brain brought no obvious benefits. Instead, it made human life even harder.

  In other apes, the brain generally accounts for only 8 percent of total energy consumption. In humans of the same period, it consumed a full 25 percent. Ancient humans had only so much food each day, so where could they find the energy to pay this much larger bill? They cut their investment in physical strength and put all their skill points into intelligence. It was rather like a country at war diverting a large share of its budget to education.

  The enlarged brain was not entirely useless, however. Early on, it provided two crucial abilities that kept ancient humans alive until its real advantages could emerge: relatively efficient social organization and the use of tools. In the wartime-country analogy, education produced capable military personnel and scientists who could design weapons.

  Homo sapiens was not the only species to develop social organization and tools. On the contrary, many human species that preceded us had already acquired both. Why, then, did only Homo sapiens reach the brain’s tipping point? Many social animals, including wolves and lions, live in organized groups. Ants, bees, and similar animals have even evolved what is known as “eusociality.” Primates such as chimpanzees also crack nuts with stones and extract termites with twigs. The brain merely amplified these two human abilities.

  For two million years of human evolution, however, all this did little more than keep our populations from dying out. Around 800,000 years ago, humans learned to use fire, and cooked food drove brain evolution further. By roughly 400,000 years ago, some archaic humans could hunt large animals with reasonable consistency.

  Before our own ancestors appeared, other human species had already mastered the skills needed for survival and occupied habitable regions across the Earth. It was like standing idle at the spawn point while everyone else had already bought their gear and taken over every part of the jungle. Only about 300,000 years ago did our ancestors, Homo sapiens, emerge in Africa, the cradle of humankind. In appearance, these early sapiens already looked much like people today.

  Early Homo sapiens quickly acquired the survival skills possessed by other human species, but that was not enough to compete with them. In Harari’s account, a revolution 70,000 years ago set every later change in motion. It enabled Homo sapiens to sweep across the globe, drive other human species to extinction, and reach places none of them had ever entered. That transformative event was the Cognitive Revolution.

  According to Harari’s hypothesis, the early Cognitive Revolution began when Homo sapiens learned to “tell tall tales.” That single ability propelled our species to the top of the food chain and consigned many other organisms, including other human species, to the evolutionary dustbin.

  The Cognitive Revolution is generally thought to have emerged first through language. One explanation is the lion theory: in the same situation, human language can convey far more information. A vervet monkey may scream to warn its companions of a lion, sending them fleeing into the trees, but the warning is indiscriminate. The others do not know where the lion is or how many lions there are. The language used by early Homo sapiens as they left Africa and spread across the world was more complex and information-rich. Someone who spotted a lion could tell the others where it was, what it was doing, and how many there were, allowing the group to decide whether to stalk and kill it or run away.

  Another explanation is the gossip theory. Once humans acquired language, they could assess other members of their group and quietly discuss their strengths and faults. That may seem pointless today, or even harmful to a tribe’s survival, but gossip has its uses. It tells us who is reliable, who is clever, and who excels at hunting or making stone spears. Because it is difficult to get to know everyone personally, this information makes the whole group more effective. Gossip lets us learn about other members more easily and cooperate with them. In a school relay, for example, hearing that one of our runners is the fastest sprinter in the school would reassure us. We may never have seen that person run, but gossip can still provide useful information.

  Whether the lion theory, the gossip theory, or some combination of the two is correct, the feature of language that ultimately carried the Cognitive Revolution forward was our ability to “tell tall tales.” This means confidently describing something that does not exist or could not happen. Humans thereby became animals capable of inventing things absent from reality. We might solemnly tell the rest of the tribe that a mountain is alive and embodies a spirit, and that unless we worship it, we will catch no prey, find no edible fruit, and locate no suitable stone for tools.

  This ability to tell tall tales is, of course, imagination expressed through language. We do not know whether our Homo sapiens ancestors first evolved language and then imagination, or first developed imagination and then learned to put it into words. We do know that once Homo sapiens could imagine, shared fictions such as a sacred mountain allowed cooperation on a much larger scale. Gossip alone can sustain groups of no more than 150 people, while wild chimpanzee communities generally contain only about 20 to 50 individuals.

Mount Kailash in Tibet, whose Tibetan name means "mountain of the gods"

  If neighboring groups shared a belief in the same sacred mountain, however, they could work together to preserve a hunting ground and drive away other tribes that entered it. With this stronger capacity for cooperation and imagination, Homo sapiens swept across the world like a flood 70,000 years ago and became its most powerful organism. So what happened to our other brothers and sisters? Genetic research now shows that it was not simply a massacre. Although most other human species became extinct, migrating Homo sapiens also had intimate encounters with Neanderthals and Denisovans. Most people alive today still carry a small amount of the blood of those brothers and sisters who disappeared tens of thousands of years ago. Homo sapiens did not replace them completely.
