  As time passed, however, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) did not adopt “Pōwehi” as the official name of M87*. The IAU’s naming remit still covers stars, planets, asteroids, and satellites, but not black holes. In academic literature and international databases, the black hole is still called M87*—the only recognized scientific name suitable for citation in a paper. “Pōwehi” instead became a “cultural name,” a symbol in public memory rather than an entry in a scientific catalogue.

And so, in scientists’ papers it remains “M87*”;
in the hearts of poets, the public, and children, it will always be “Pōwehi.”
A dark source named by humanity, a void illuminated by language.

References

  1. https://www.livescience.com/65223-black-hole-names.html
  2. http://wenhui.news365.com.cn/html/2019-04/15/content_778903.html
  3. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_Observatory
  4. https://apod.nasa.gov/apod/ap190329.html、https://apod.nasa.gov/apod/ap180309.html
  5. IAU, Naming of Astronomical Objects Policy, 2021.

entry.title: Salvation
entry.content:
Salvation

Author: 观复·钧天

  Salvation is the pursuit of a higher material or spiritual state by people dissatisfied with their present condition. It begins with an awareness that one must save oneself. Along the way, the external force of “salvation by others” may either help or hinder that effort. Its outcome is deliverance, and the highest form of deliverance is awakening: recognizing that things have always been as they are, that free will is as it is, that the natural environment is as it is, and that the course of history is as it is.

  Within finite time and space, salvation is indispensable and runs through the whole of human existence. Humanity confronts the infinite with the finite: finite time and space face infinite time and space; finite perception faces infinite vastness; a finite system of knowledge faces an infinite one. In Free and Easy Wandering, Zhuangzi writes, “Small understanding cannot reach great understanding; a short life cannot know a long life.” The small cannot comprehend the great, while the great can contain and understand the small. Human beings continually move from the small toward the great, approaching facts and truth one step at a time. Our awareness of self-salvation is a kind of “rational fatalism.” Humanity fails in its confrontation with fate because of “the contradiction between finite and infinite knowledge.” In this sense, every act of salvation is a movement toward the infinite, a shedding of delusion, and a step closer to facts and truth.

  Yet humanity also regards itself as the most intelligent of all beings in the Universe, and there is something moving about our advance toward the infinite. We do not march proudly in triumph, because the future can never be fully known. Nor do we sink into sorrow and despair, because people always retain a spiritual impulse to rise. What we feel is closer to a blend of sadness and excitement: we know that we are entering an unknown infinity, even as we know that any of it may or may not be true. We cannot know whether we will succeed. And so we simply keep walking, onward into the infinite.

  Beyond desire lie spiritual needs that distinguish humans from animals. These needs exist at different levels, but the most basic are shared to some extent; what varies is how people satisfy them. Some say that spiritual needs are social and psychological needs. Strictly speaking, that is not quite accurate. They do have a social dimension and a diachronic one. They also carry a degree of personal subjectivity, as the need for art shows: some people are drawn to music, some to painting, and others to sculpture. None of this changes the fact that humanity’s most basic spiritual needs are universal. They have existed throughout human history and are present in everyone. People in every age, including you and me, encounter these needs at different levels. What can satisfy them? Facing them directly; obtaining what can fulfill us; and awakening—recognizing our own needs, understanding what they are and how they may be met, and grasping our lives through thought and being. Zhuangzi and his celebrated Free and Easy Wandering and “Zhuang Zhou Dreams of Being a Butterfly”

entry.title: EHT Set to Unveil the First-Ever Image of a Black Hole
entry.content:
A still from a video simulation showing what a black hole's shadow might look like. The video was produced by Peter Galison and Chyld King for a short film about the Event Horizon Telescope project. The first image of a black hole will be unveiled at a press conference at 9:00 a.m. EDT on April 10, 2019 (9:00 p.m. Beijing time).

Image: © EHT Outreach/YouTube

  The EHT recently announced a press conference for April 10, 2019. Its statement read in part:

  On April 10, 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration will hold simultaneous press conferences in several regions around the world to present its latest research results, together with numerous events organized by researchers and affiliated institutions. The press conferences will take place simultaneously in Brussels (English), Lyngby (Danish), Santiago (Spanish), Shanghai (Chinese), Tokyo (Japanese), Taipei (Chinese), and Washington (English), beginning at 13:00 UTC (21:00 Beijing time).

  The Shanghai Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Taiwan’s Academia Sinica Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics also announced local press conferences.

Shanghai Astronomical Observatory, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Academia Sinica Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics

  The press conferences across six countries and regions will begin at 9:00 p.m. Beijing time on April 10. Astronomers are excited because a black hole’s gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. Its pull sends nearby objects into rapid orbits, and observations of those objects have made the case for black holes widely accepted. Yet no one has ever truly “seen” one. The star S0-2 completes an orbit in 15.2 years and reaches nearly 3% of the speed of light, or 9,000 kilometers per second. For comparison, the Solar System takes about 230 million years to orbit the center of the Milky Way at only about 250 kilometers per second.

  Despite its name, the Event Horizon Telescope is not one enormous instrument. It is a network of eight radio telescopes in Hawaii, Arizona, Spain, Mexico, Chile, and Antarctica. In April 2017, the network observed two giants: Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, and an even larger black hole in the galaxy M87, 53.5 million light-years away. After nearly two years of processing the data, the team is preparing to release its first black-hole images this April.

This artist's impression depicts a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole surrounded by an accretion disk. A star has been torn apart by the black hole's tidal forces, and the accretion disk consists largely of the star's remains. Heat generated during accretion produces a gamma-ray burst resembling a supernova explosion.

Image: © ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser/N. Bartmann

  Black holes are extraordinarily hard to observe. “Finding a black hole is about as difficult as trying to find and observe an orange placed on the Moon from Earth,” said Sheperd Doeleman, director of the Event Horizon Telescope project. A black hole may dwarf a planet or a person, but against the Milky Way it is minuscule, making its event horizon extremely difficult to image. “The EHT’s target is roughly 10% the size of our Solar System,” University of Amsterdam astrophysicist Sera Markoff said during a panel discussion. Doeleman added, “Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, is only about the size of Mercury’s orbit.” The Milky Way is around 50 billion times larger than Sagittarius A*. Even from a vantage point outside the galaxy, picking out the black hole among its billions of stars and planets would be daunting.

This artist's image depicts a simulation of a black hole's accretion disk, along with simulated images of three possible event-horizon shapes.

Image: © ESO/N. Bartmann/A. Broderick/C.K. Chan/D. Psaltis/F. Ozel

  “At the heart of the project, 200 scientists want to answer two questions,” said University of Arizona astronomer and physicist Psaltis. “The first is simple: is it possible to photograph a black hole? Their second question is the important one. Scientists want to know whether Einstein’s theory of black holes is completely correct. A hundred years ago, Einstein told us what the size and shape of a black hole’s horizon should be. If we can place a measuring ‘ruler’ across the horizon, we can test Einstein’s theory of black holes.”

Gargantua, the black hole in the film *Interstellar*, created by the London visual-effects company Double Negative.

Image:AF ARCHIVE/ALAMY STOCK PHOTO

  Fiction tends to portray black holes more imaginatively. Gargantua, for example, serves as a time-travel plot device in Interstellar. No one yet knows whether the image reconstructed from EHT data will resemble the film’s elaborate CGI. Beyond making an accurate image of the horizon, scientists hope the observations will reveal more about the physics of black holes.

  “Because LIGO—the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory—has found that the spacetime around black holes closely matches Einstein’s predictions from relativity, I hope the EHT data will pin down the physical details of how gas accretes onto and is ejected from around supermassive black holes,” said Abraham Loeb, professor and chair of astronomy at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics. “A century after the theory of black holes was formulated mathematically, people are about to see the face of a black hole for the first time. Karl Schwarzschild and Albert Einstein would surely be thrilled if they could see this image.”

Appendix: Livestreams for anyone eager to watch (a VPN may be required):

  1. Shanghai (Chinese): (The Shanghai link does not require a VPN. Follow the “Read the original” link at the end of the article to enter the stream.) http://www.xinhuanet.com/politics/ksh/zhibo/201904/3731328_m.html?type=mobile

  2. Taipei (Chinese): https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=_GsTBTenBZY&feature=youtu.be

  3. Washington (English): https://m.youtube.com/c/VideosatNSF/live

  4. Brussels (English): https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=Dr20f19czeE&reload=9

  5. Tokyo (Japanese): https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=_QBQMT5vrJo

References

  1. Space.com:https://www.space.com/event-horizon-telescope-is-trying-to-photograph-black-holes.html

  2. Science:https://www.sciencemag.org/news/2019/04/here-s-what-scientists-think-black-hole-looks

  3. EHT:https://eventhorizontelescope.org/science

  4. SaLon.com:https://www.salon.com/2019/02/03/scientists-are-on-the-verge-of-imaging-a-black-holes-shadow-for-the-first-time/

  5. Official websites: Shanghai Astronomical Observatory, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Academia Sinica Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics

entry.title: Did You Know? Moderate Drinking Can Carry a Cancer Risk Comparable to Smoking
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

  A British study found that the additional cancer risk associated with drinking one bottle of wine per week was roughly equivalent to smoking 5 cigarettes per week for men and 10 for women. The researchers used data from nonsmokers and compared the risks with an epidemiological model.

  The study, published in the British journal BMC Public Health on March 28, 2019, was among the first to estimate the relationship between alcohol and cigarettes in terms of cancer risk.

Credit: Shutterstock

  The study aimed to communicate the cancer risks of moderate drinking more effectively. Moderate alcohol consumption is widely believed to be less harmful than smoking, but research in the United States and the United Kingdom has found that many people are unaware of the connection between alcohol and cancer. A 2017 survey by the American Society of Clinical Oncology, for example, found that roughly 70% of Americans did not know that alcohol consumption was a carcinogenic risk factor.

  “We estimated the number of cigarettes that would carry the same cancer risk as a bottle of wine,” said Dr. Theresa Hydes of gastroenterology and hepatology at University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust, the study’s lead author. “This lets us communicate the potential cancer risk of drinking more intuitively by drawing on what people already know about the harms of smoking. By using cigarettes as a comparison, we hope to help people make better-informed lifestyle choices.” This inventive comparison offers a useful way to help people understand the carcinogenic risk of alcohol more accurately.

  It is important to note, however, that the study did not claim that moderate drinking and smoking carried identical carcinogenic risks. It considered only the cancer risk associated with drinking and did not account for other health effects. It also assessed lifetime cancer risk in the general population, which may differ from the risk faced by a particular person who smokes or drinks.

Alcohol and cigarettes

  The study set out to answer a question: in terms of cancer risk, how many cigarettes are equivalent to drinking one bottle of wine containing approximately 80 grams of pure alcohol? Using data on cancer risk in the general British population and previously published research on the relationships among alcohol, smoking, and cancer, the researchers estimated that among nonsmokers, drinking one bottle of wine per week increased men’s lifetime cancer risk by 1.0% and women’s by 1.4%. Put another way, if 1,000 men and 1,000 women each drank a bottle of wine every week, about 10 of the men and 14 of the women might later develop cancer because of their drinking. The higher risk among women was mainly due to the close association between alcohol consumption and breast cancer. The effect was equivalent to smoking 5 cigarettes per week for men and 10 for women.

A “carcinogen we all know”

  “Most people know that cigarettes cause cancer,” Seitz said. “It is useful for the public to hear that a certain amount of alcohol carries the same cancer risk as a certain number of cigarettes.” He also noted that although alcohol is a known carcinogen, its associated cancer risks are rarely discussed. Some dietary guidelines even recommend a daily quantity of alcoholic drinks. “If I did not call it alcohol, wine, beer, or cocktails and simply called it a carcinogen,” Seitz said, “no one would ask how many glasses of carcinogen you plan to drink.”

  The researchers also noted that because the study considered only cancer risk, it did not account for other illnesses associated with smoking or drinking, such as respiratory, cardiovascular, or liver disease.

  Although 5 to 10 cigarettes per week may not sound like many, smokers typically consume far more. British smokers, for example, average about 80 cigarettes per week, while smokers in the United States consume about 100 per person each week. Nevertheless, the researchers emphasized that “these findings show that the health risks of moderate drinking are an important public-health issue.”

Reference

  1. https://www.livescience.com/65092-alcohol-cigarettes-cancer-risk.html

entry.title: Earth at the Spring Equinox, Seen from Space
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

At Earth's spring equinox, the illuminated and dark hemispheres are almost equal in area. | Credit: NOAA; NOAA Environmental Visualization Laboratory

  On March 20, 2019, a GOES satellite photographed Earth at the spring equinox. In the image, half the planet is bathed in light while the other half lies in darkness, like a black-and-white cookie.

  This beautiful symmetry will not surprise anyone familiar with astronomy and geography. Yet a real photograph—especially an astronomical one—can be more powerful than the theories we learn, leaving us in awe of the universe’s extraordinary beauty. In Latin, “equinox” means “equal night.” As geography teachers tell us, the spring and autumn equinoxes occur in March and September each year, when day and night are nearly equal in length at every latitude.

  Earth’s rotation axis is tilted 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane. The subsolar point moves between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, so sunlight is usually distributed unevenly across the planet. Depending on Earth’s position in its orbit around the Sun, day and night are generally unequal in length in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

  “At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the Northern and Southern Hemispheres receive essentially the same amount of daylight,” said C. Alex Young, associate director for science in the Heliophysics Science Division at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. In other words, at noon on an equinox, the Sun is directly overhead at the equator.

  The 2019 spring equinox occurred at 5:58 a.m. Beijing time on March 21, marking the first astronomical day of spring in the Northern Hemisphere. GOES-East captured the image above at 8:00 p.m. Beijing time on March 20, 2019.

  The GOES series—the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite system—is a network of Earth-observation satellites operated by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). One satellite is stationed at 75° west longitude and another at 135° west, hence the names GOES-East and GOES-West. Together, they cover roughly one-third of the globe and provide continuous meteorological observations of the Western Hemisphere 24 hours a day.

References

  1. https://www.livescience.com/65057-spring-equinox-from-space.html

entry.title: Suicide: The Only Serious Philosophical Problem
entry.content:
Author: Guanfu · Juntian

  Camus opens The Myth of Sisyphus by declaring suicide the only serious philosophical problem: deciding whether life is worth living is itself an answer to a philosophical question. His philosophy is therefore centered on individual life, not merely on the external world.

  One point needs to be clear: when Camus says that “suicide is the only serious philosophical problem,” he is by no means urging anyone to take their own life. He once wrote: “The absence of hope is not the same as despair; lucidity does not lead to submission. A person should recognize that life is their only wealth: it must inevitably pass away, yet it can also be developed to the fullest possible extent. A person should, and can, find the courage to live in this world—even happiness.” Camus addressed these words to people thinking of giving up their lives. He raised the question of suicide to make us consider the meaning of life and how to face the absurd: the world’s impenetrability and strangeness.

  The subtitle of The Myth of Sisyphus is “An Essay on the Absurd.” What, then, is the absurd?

  In the second chapter of The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus describes the absurd as “a wall.” He writes: “Rising, streetcar, four hours in the office or the factory, meal, streetcar, four hours of work, meal, sleep; Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, according to the same rhythm—this path is easily followed most of the time. But one day the ‘why’ arises, and everything begins in that weariness tinged with amazement.”

  “Why?” I suspect many people have asked themselves that question. The absurd often lies in the conflict between our desire for meaning and the world’s inability to satisfy it. Anyone who can still ask “why” has encountered the absurd, but has also opened a door to resisting it.

  Unfortunately, most people around us do not usually ask “why.” The Stranger begins with the famous line: “Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday.” Many people spend their entire lives estranged from everything they do, even from their own lives.

  I often hear people say that even a wretched life is better than a good death. Camus would answer that even in a wretched life, a person will still ask questions. No one can escape this one: Why am I alive? “The world’s impenetrability and strangeness—this is the absurd.”

Three Possible Responses to the Absurd

  Camus sees three possible responses to the absurd:

  The first is straightforward: suicide, the ending of one’s life. Someone who believes life has no meaning or value may choose it. In Camus’s view, however, suicide does not resolve the absurd. It removes the person and thereby evades the problem. This is the coward’s way out, not an act of genuine revolt.

  The second is to seek a transcendent world through religion. For Camus, answering the absurd with a transcendent explanation means surrendering the courage to confront it; this is “philosophical suicide.” He regards the approach as another form of self-destruction. Religion, then, offers no viable way past the absurd.

  The third possibility is to accept the absurd. For Camus, this is the only authentic and effective answer. “Acceptance” here does not mean passive submission. It means facing the absurd with open eyes and creating one’s own meaning and value within meaninglessness. Camus wrote: “There is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn.” The line captures the heart of Sisyphus’s attitude: even if fate is fixed, we can still rise above it through the stance we take. Walking back down the mountain, Sisyphus knows the stone will roll down again, yet he chooses to climb once more. Resistance remains possible precisely where it seems impossible. Sisyphus, in other words, embodies humanity’s ultimate revolt against fate.

entry.title: The Coolest Members of the Particle Family
entry.content:
Author: 一毫秒的永恒

  Physics is full of particles such as neutrons and photons, but the particle world is stranger than most people imagine. Its members come in different sizes, behave in different ways, and bear memorable names ranging from supersymmetric particles to the “God particle.” Today, let us meet some of the coolest members of this extraordinary family.

Higgs Boson

  The Higgs boson is enormously important to physics. Often nicknamed the “God particle,” it is tied to the origin of mass for many elementary particles. In 1964, physicists were trying to understand why some particles were more massive than others and where their mass came from. Peter Higgs proposed what became known as the Higgs mechanism. The boson is associated with the Higgs field, which the mechanism assumes permeates the universe. Together, the field and the boson are thought to account for the masses of many fundamental particles. Scientists hoped the mechanism would solve the puzzle and complete the Standard Model, our current description of known particles. In 2012, experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC) confirmed the discovery of a particle with properties consistent with those of the Higgs boson, providing crucial support for the Standard Model. The LHC continues to collect data as researchers investigate the Higgs field and boson in greater detail.

A visualization reconstructing particle tracks after a collision at the Large Hadron Collider | Credit: CERN

Neutrino

  Neutrinos are subatomic particles with extremely little mass, and they rarely interact with ordinary matter. They usually travel at close to the speed of light. Trillions pass through your body at any given moment, yet so few interact with normal matter that they leave almost no detectable trace. Neutrinos are produced by the Sun, cosmic rays, and radioactive decay inside Earth. Their antiparticles are called antineutrinos; under certain conditions, neutrinos and antineutrinos can annihilate one another.

A solar flare at the moment of eruption, imaged at a wavelength of 94 ångströms | Credits: NASA/SDO/GSFC

Sparticle

  “Sparticle” is short for “supersymmetric particle,” a term from the theory of supersymmetry. The theory proposes that every known particle has an undiscovered partner: every fermion should have a bosonic partner, and every boson a fermionic one. The electron’s supersymmetric partner, for example, is the selectron; the quark’s is the squark.

  As of 2026, no sparticle has been found experimentally. Why do we not see these particles in the universe? Scientists think they may be far more massive than ordinary particles, and massive, unstable particles generally decay very quickly. A sparticle, in other words, would vanish almost as soon as it was created. Producing one requires the extraordinary energies found shortly after the Big Bang, although a large particle accelerator such as the LHC might be able to re-create them. To explain why sparticles should be so heavy, physicists have suggested that a hidden sector of the universe, beyond direct detection, may cause supersymmetry to break. We could neither see nor touch such a sector, only sense it through its interactions.

Fermilab's CDF (Collider Detector at Fermilab) | Credit: Fermilab

Graviton

  The graviton is a hypothetical particle in theories of quantum gravity and a possible carrier of the gravitational interaction. In quantum field theory, fundamental interactions can often be described as exchanges of particles. Electromagnetism, for example, is mediated by photons, massless particles that carry the electromagnetic force. By analogy, scientists have proposed that particles called gravitons may mediate gravity.

  As of 2026, no graviton has been detected experimentally, so its existence remains theoretical. Gravitons would interact so weakly with matter that directly detecting even one is thought to be nearly impossible under realistic physical conditions. One study calculated that even a detector as massive as Jupiter, operating at 100% efficiency in a close orbit around a neutron star, would detect only about one graviton every ten years under the most favorable conditions.

Artist's impression of gravitational waves | Credit: NASA

Antimatter

  Antimatter is made of antiparticles, the counterparts of the particles in ordinary matter. When matter and antimatter meet, they annihilate each other, releasing enormous energy in accordance with E=mc². The process has an exceptionally high energy density. Scientists believe that every ordinary particle has a corresponding antiparticle with the same mass but the opposite charge. The positron, for example, is the electron’s antiparticle: its electric charge has the same magnitude but the opposite sign.

Artist's concept of antimatter produced by a thunderstorm | Credits: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center

Quark

  Quarks are elementary particles proposed by Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig. They participate in the strong interaction and are the basic constituents of hadrons such as protons and neutrons. Gell-Mann took the word “quark” from a line in James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake: “Three quarks for Muster Mark.” Quarks always occur in combinations because the force binding them grows as the distance between them increases. Separating them would require so much energy that free quarks do not occur in nature. Six types, or “flavors,” of quark are known: up (u), down (d), strange (s), charm ©, bottom (b), and top (t). A proton, for example, contains two up quarks and one down quark, while a neutron contains two down quarks and one up quark. Up and down quarks are the least massive. Heavier quarks rapidly turn into up or down quarks through particle decay. Because those heavier quarks are generally unstable, strange, charm, top, and bottom quarks can be produced only in high-energy particle collisions, such as those involving cosmic rays or particle accelerators, and decay soon afterward.

A reconstructed lead-nucleus collision recorded by the ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider.The experiment studies quark–gluon plasma, a state of matter that existed moments after the Big Bang | Credits: CERN

  That concludes our tour of these remarkable particles. Which one is your favorite? Does the universe seem a little more astonishing now that you have seen some of its variety? If you want every question answered, keep searching for the answers yourself.

References

  1. https://www.livescience.com/13593-exotic-particles-sparticles-antimatter-god-particle.html
  2. Wikipedia: “Higgs boson,” “Quark,” “Superpartner,” “Neutrino,” “Antimatter,” and “Graviton”

entry.title: Did Neptune's Tiny Moon Come from Proteus?
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

“A Moon That Shouldn’t Exist”

Artist's concept of Hippocamp, the tiny moon discovered by the Hubble Space Telescope in 2013. This was the first evidence that a moon may have splintered from a larger parent body after a comet strike. | Credit: NASA, ESA and J. Olmsted (STScI)

  After several years of analysis, a team of planetary scientists finally had an explanation for the mysterious Neptunian moon they discovered with the Hubble Space Telescope in 2013.

  The tiny moon, named Hippocamp, orbits unusually close to the much larger Proteus. Ordinarily, a moon as large as Proteus should clear smaller moons from its path or draw them in through its gravity.

  So why is Hippocamp still there? It is probably a fragment of Proteus, knocked loose when a comet struck the larger moon billions of years ago. Hippocamp is only 20 miles (about 34 kilometers) across and has just one-thousandth the mass of Proteus, whose diameter is about 260 miles (about 418 kilometers).

  “The first thing we realized was that you would not expect to find such a tiny moon right next to Neptune’s largest inner moon,” said Mark Showalter of the SETI Institute in Mountain View, California. “In the distant past, as the larger moon slowly migrated outward, Proteus was once where Hippocamp is now.”

  Images taken by Voyager 2 in 1989 support this idea. They show a vast impact crater on Proteus, nearly large enough to have shattered the moon. “In 1989, we thought the huge depression must simply be a crater,” Showalter said. “With Hubble, we now know that a small piece of Proteus was left behind—the object we know today as Hippocamp.” The moons’ orbits are now 7,500 miles (about 12,070 kilometers) apart.

Observations of Hippocamp (inside the white square). The Hubble Space Telescope took the images in sequence: (a) 2004, (b) 2005, (c) 2009, and (d) 2016.

  The history of Neptune’s moon system has been both violent and complicated. Billions of years ago, Neptune captured its large moon Triton from the Kuiper Belt, a densely populated, disk-shaped region beyond Neptune’s orbit filled with icy and rocky bodies. Triton’s gravity disrupted Neptune’s original family of moons before it settled into a relatively stable circular orbit. Debris from the shattered moons then came back together to form a second generation. Later comet impacts continued to break those moons apart and may have created Hippocamp, a possible third-generation moon.

  “Based on estimates of the enormous number of comets, it is fairly clear that other moons in the outer Solar System have been struck and disrupted by comets many times, then reassembled, in a cycle that repeats over and over,” said Jack Lissauer of NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, California, a coauthor of the new study. “Proteus and Hippocamp provide a somewhat dramatic example of how moons are sometimes broken into several pieces by comets.”

Diagram of the orbits of Neptune's moons, with Hippocamp's orbit highlighted. | Credit:NASA, ESA, and A. Feild (STScI) | From:https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocamp_(moon)#/media

  Hippocamp, originally designated S/2004 N 1, is about 34 kilometers (20 miles) across and completes an orbit of Neptune in less than one Earth day. Its discovery on July 1, 2013, raised the number of known Neptunian moons to 14. Hippocamp was too faint for Voyager 2 to see when the probe flew past Neptune and its moons in 1989. Mark Showalter of the SETI Institute found it by analyzing archival Hubble images taken between 2004 and 2009.

  The moon received the formal designation Neptune XIV on September 25, 2018, and the name Hippocamp in February 2019.

  The name Hippocamp comes from a horse-headed, fish-tailed creature in Greek mythology. The seahorse’s scientific name is Hippocampus, also the name of an important brain region involved in memory. Under International Astronomical Union rules, Neptune’s moons must be named for creatures from the undersea worlds of Greek and Roman mythology.

References

  1. ScienceDaily: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2019/02/190221095033.htm
  2. Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocamp_(moon)

entry.title: SpaceX Rocket Launches First Privately Funded Lunar Lander
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

  At 9:45 a.m. Beijing time on February 22, 2019, just as the Moon rose above the horizon, a Falcon 9 rocket set off toward it.

  On the evening of February 21, 2019, a previously flown SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket successfully launched an Israeli lunar lander and an Indonesian communications satellite from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in the United States. After placing both payloads into orbit, Falcon 9’s first stage returned to Earth and landed safely on the uncrewed drone ship Of Course I Still Love You in the Atlantic Ocean.

  Although the mission’s primary payload was Indonesia’s Nusantara Satu satellite, the small lunar lander riding along as a secondary payload stole the spotlight. It became not only Israel’s first spacecraft to venture beyond Earth orbit, but also the first privately funded lunar lander.

Concept art of the Beresheet lander on the lunar surface | Credit: SpaceIL

  Today’s launch marks an important moment for Israel. Apart from several communications and Earth-observation satellites, the country had never launched a mission beyond Earth orbit.

  The lander is named Beresheet, Hebrew for “beginning.” It was built by SpaceIL, an Israeli nonprofit that entered the Google Lunar X Prize in 2011. The international competition offered 30 million US dollars to any privately funded team that could land a robotic spacecraft on the Moon. If no team met the deadline, the competition would have no winner.

  “Our vision is to show the world the best that Israel has to offer,” SpaceIL donor Sylvan Adams said at a briefing in Orlando, Florida, on February 20, 2019. “Israel is about to become the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon. That is an extraordinary achievement.”

Beresheet will orbit Earth repeatedly for about 27 days to build the momentum it needs.

  Beresheet will take seven weeks to reach the Moon. Before arriving, it will circle Earth several times, using Earth’s gravity to gain the momentum it needs to reach its destination. If Beresheet makes a successful soft landing, Israel will become the fourth country to achieve one on the Moon, following the United States, Russia, and China. In 1966, the Soviet spacecraft Luna 9 made the first soft landing on the Moon. Later that year, NASA’s Surveyor 1 landed on the lunar surface. China’s Chang’e 3 lander and Yutu rover joined them in 2013.

  When Beresheet approaches the lunar surface, it will aim for the region known as Mare Tranquillitatis, SpaceIL spacecraft program manager Yigal Harel said at the briefing. The spacecraft, however, will be able to operate for only about two days before running out of power. During that time, it will study the Moon’s magnetic field and photograph the lunar surface.

  Even after those two days, the defunct spacecraft will not be entirely useless. Beresheet carries a laser retroreflector, a mirror-like device that requires no power and enables space-to-ground communication through NASA’s Deep Space Network (DSN). NASA provided the device for the mission, and the agreement will allow the startup to use the DSN during its lunar mission.

  The reflector is not the only payload aboard Beresheet built to endure. SpaceIL also created a time capsule filled with digital files about the spacecraft and a range of Israeli mementos. These include the Hebrew Bible, Hebrew songs, artwork by Israeli children, and photographs of Ilan Ramon, Israel’s first and only astronaut. The capsule also contains a vast digital database known as the “Lunar Library,” a project of the nonprofit Arch Mission Foundation. “The library holds millions of documents from around the world, including many different dictionaries and encyclopedias, as well as three laser-etched coins,” said SpaceIL cofounder Yonatan Winetraub. “It will be the most information-dense artifact ever to reach the Moon, and after arriving in 2019, it will remain there so that future generations can see what life on Earth was like.”

This small coin is part of the time capsule aboard Beresheet. The entire Hebrew Bible is laser-etched onto its surface. | Credits: Hanneke Weitering/Space.com

  Beresheet and Nusantara Satu launched aboard a Falcon 9 booster that had already flown two separate missions to space, making this its third successful launch and landing. SpaceX had first flown and recovered the same first-stage booster for a third time during the SSO-A mission in December 2018; the Nusantara Satu mission was the company’s second time reaching that milestone. The booster may also be refurbished for a historic fourth flight. Reusing rocket boosters can drastically reduce the cost of spaceflight, one of SpaceX’s central goals.

Note: Beresheet attempted to land on April 11, 2019, but lost contact after its main engine failed during the final stage of descent. It ultimately crashed onto the lunar surface in the early hours of that day, Beijing time.

entry.title: Underwater Archaeologists Uncover Surprising Artifacts from a Roman Naval Battle
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

The Naval Battle

  Archaeologists have explored the site of a naval battle fought between Rome and Carthage 2,200 years ago. Their discoveries offer clues to how the battle unfolded, along with several mysteries that remain unsolved.

Archaeologists found numerous helmets while surveying the Roman–Carthaginian battlefield. This 3D model of one helmet was created by William M. Murray. | Credit: Courtesy of RPM Nautical Foundation

  The finds suggest that Carthage reused captured Roman warships in the battle. They also indicate that Carthaginian sailors may have thrown their cargo overboard in a desperate attempt to escape Roman pursuit.

  Historical records place the naval battle on March 10, 241 BCE, near the Aegadian Islands off Sicily in the Mediterranean. A Carthaginian fleet was trying to deliver supplies to Carthaginian forces on Sicily when the Roman navy intercepted it and destroyed most of its ships. Rome won a decisive victory, forcing Carthage to seek peace and accept terms favorable to Rome.

  Over the past decade, underwater archaeologists have surveyed the battlefield and recovered bronze rams, metal helmets, and fragments of ceramic vessels. The final field season of 2018 alone yielded six bronze rams, several helmets, and pieces of pottery.

Carthaginian and Roman Ships in Combat

A Roman bronze ram found during the survey of the battlefield. | Credit: Photo by William M. Murray, courtesy of RPM Nautical Foundation

  Carthage appears to have entered the battle with a fleet that included captured Roman ships rather than confronting Rome with an entirely Carthaginian force. “Of the 19 bronze rams already found in this area, I believe 11 are Roman,” said team member William Murray, a professor of Greek history at the University of South Florida. Many of the helmets found at the site also belong to a design archaeologists call the Montefortino type. This helmet was so popular in Rome that the Romans decorated some bronze rams with its image.

  The large number of Roman rams and Montefortino-style helmets has left archaeologists with a puzzle. “You would expect the Carthaginians, who lost the battle, to have suffered heavy casualties,” Murray said. “But you might also expect some of the bronze rams to have come from warships crewed by Carthaginians.”

  “Carthage probably used ships that it had captured from the Romans in an earlier naval battle,” Murray said. Historical records show that Carthage captured 93 Roman ships in a battle several years before the Battle of the Aegadian Islands. The abundance of Montefortino helmets remains harder to explain. “One explanation is that the Carthaginians hired mercenaries from Gaul and Iberia to crew many of the ships in their fleet, and soldiers from those regions sometimes used Montefortino helmets,” Murray said.

A Roman bronze ram found during the survey bears the image of a winged woman. She is Victoria, the Roman goddess of victory. | Credit: Photo by William M. Murray, courtesy of RPM Nautical Foundation

Did the Sailors Throw Their Cargo into the Sea?

  The archaeologists also found amphorae, oval ceramic jars with two handles that were often used to store liquids, scattered around the remains of Roman ships. Murray found this strange because jars that fell from a ship’s storage area should have landed in clusters. “It is as if they were thrown into the sea, which separated them before they sank to the seabed,” Murray said. “One possible explanation is that the Carthaginian sailors realized during the battle that their mission would fail and jettisoned their cargo—the supplies intended for Carthaginian forces in Sicily—to make their ships lighter, faster, and better able to escape the Roman fleet.”

Wasted Food?

  “Besides being widely scattered, none of the amphorae has the tar-like lining that would keep liquids from evaporating during storage,” Murray said. Most of the liquid would therefore have evaporated by the time the jars reached Sicily. Even if the Carthaginian fleet had made it there, part of the cargo would have gone to waste. Amphorae could also hold grain, Murray noted, but ancient accounts of unloading ships suggest that grain was more often carried in sacks.

  “Perhaps the Carthaginians were in such a hurry to supply their army that they had no time to choose suitable containers,” Murray said. “Another possibility is that they did not have many sacks available, so they decided to carry dry goods to Sicily in amphorae.” Scientists are running chemical tests to determine what the containers held.

  Murray and other members of the research team presented their findings in a paper at the joint annual meeting of the Archaeological Institute of America and the Society for Classical Studies, held in San Diego from January 3 through 6.

  Sicily’s Soprintendenza del Mare and the RPM Nautical Foundation jointly run the project to survey and excavate the underwater site, with scientists from several other institutions also taking part. The team plans another field expedition in 2019.

References

  1. https://www.livescience.com/64734-underwater-rome-carthage-battle-artifacts.html

entry.title: Farewell, Opportunity: Remembering a Mars Exploration Pioneer
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

  A record-setting NASA mission on Mars has come to an end. One of the longest-running and most successful feats in interplanetary exploration, the Opportunity rover mission concluded after nearly fifteen years on the Martian surface. Its legacy laid the groundwork for NASA’s return to Mars.

  In June 2018, a severe planet-wide dust storm blanketed Opportunity’s location on Mars, and the rover stopped communicating with Earth. Engineers at the Space Flight Operations Facility at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) sent more than 1,000 recovery commands in an effort to reestablish contact, but none succeeded. The solar-powered rover last communicated on June 10, 2018.

  NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine said, “It is because of trailblazing missions such as Opportunity that there will come a day when our brave astronauts walk on the surface of Mars.” He added, “And when that day arrives, some portion of that first footprint will be owned by the men and women of Opportunity, and a little rover that defied the odds and did so much in the name of exploration.”

  Opportunity was designed to operate for only 90 days and travel 1,000 meters. Its endurance, scientific value, and longevity exceeded every expectation. It lasted sixty times longer than planned, and by the time it reached its final resting place in Perseverance Valley, it had traveled more than 45 kilometers.

  Thomas Zurbuchen, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, said, “For more than a decade, Opportunity has been an icon in the field of planetary exploration, teaching us about Mars’ ancient past as a potentially habitable planet, and revealing uncharted Martian landscapes.” He continued, “Whatever loss we feel now must be tempered with the knowledge that the legacy of Opportunity continues—both on the surface of Mars with the Curiosity rover and InSight lander—and in the clean rooms of JPL.”

During a presentation, Opportunity principal investigator Steve Squyres points to a strange rock that the rover found on January 8, 2014, named "Pinnacle Island." The image on the left side of the screen was taken by Opportunity on December 26, 2013. The rover on the right is Curiosity, the first nuclear-powered Mars rover. | Credit: NASA/JPL

  JPL Mars Exploration Rover project manager John Callas said, “We have made every reasonable engineering effort to try to recover Opportunity and have determined that the likelihood of receiving a signal is far too low to continue recovery efforts.”

  Opportunity landed in Mars’s Meridiani Planum region on January 24, 2004, seven months after launching from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. Its twin rover, Spirit, had landed more than twenty days earlier in the 166-kilometer-wide Gusev Crater on the other side of Mars. Spirit traveled nearly eight kilometers before its mission ended in May 2011.

  From the day Opportunity landed, a team of mission engineers, rover drivers, and scientists on Earth worked together to overcome one challenge after another and move the rover between geological sites on Mars. They plotted safe routes across rough terrain so that the 174-kilogram Martian explorer could maneuver around rocks and boulders. At times, it climbed gravel-covered slopes as steep as 32 degrees—an off-world record—explored crater floors and hilltops, and crossed what may once have been riverbeds. Its final journey took it to the western edge of Perseverance Valley.

  JPL Director Michael Watkins said, “I cannot think of a more appropriate place for Opportunity to endure on the surface of Mars than one called Perseverance Valley. The records, discoveries and sheer tenacity of this intrepid little rover are a testament to the ingenuity, dedication and perseverance of the people who built and guided her.”

  Opportunity had already lost steering in one front wheel in 2005. A stuck heater severely limited the power available to the rover, and a Martian sand ripple nearly trapped it for good. Two years later, a dust storm lasting two months put the rover in danger. Opportunity lost its 256-megabyte flash memory in 2015 and steering in its other front wheel in 2017. Whenever it encountered an obstacle, the team on Earth found a way around it and kept the rover operating. The massive dust storm that formed in the summer of 2018, however, proved too much even for the most seasoned Mars explorer in history.

  Callas said, “When I think of Opportunity, I will recall that place on Mars where our intrepid rover far exceeded everyone’s expectations. But what I suppose I’ll cherish most is the impact Opportunity had on us here on Earth. It’s the accomplished exploration and phenomenal discoveries. It’s the generation of young scientists and engineers who became space explorers with this mission. It’s the technical legacy of the Mars Exploration Rovers, which is carried aboard Curiosity and the upcoming Mars 2020 mission. Farewell, Opportunity, and well done.”

Distances traveled by Opportunity and other extraterrestrial vehicles, as of February 13, 2019. Opportunity ranks first at 45.16 kilometers.Second: the Soviet Union's Lunokhod 2, which landed on the Moon in 1973 and held the off-world driving record for many years.Third: the United States' Apollo 17 lunar rover.Fourth: the United States' Apollo 15 lunar rover.Fifth: the United States' Apollo 16 lunar rover.Sixth: the United States' Curiosity Mars rover.Seventh: the Soviet Union's Lunokhod 1.Eighth: the United States' Spirit Mars rover.Ninth: the United States' Sojourner Mars rover.Tenth: China's Yutu 2.Eleventh: China's Yutu 1.Credit: MARS.NASA.GOV

References

  1. https://www.nasa.gov/press-release/nasas-record-setting-opportunity-rover-mission-on-mars-comes-to-end
  2. https://www.space.com/mars-rovers-after-opportunity.html
  3. https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-019-00575-2
  4. https://www.space.com/27-latest-mars-shots-spirit-opportunity/2.html
  5. https://www.borntoengineer.com/nasa-mars-opportunity-rover-records-dead

entry.title: Forget The Wandering Earth: How to Destroy the Planet in Three Elegant Steps
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

Concept art of an asteroid impact | Credit: Don Davis/NASA

  For years, certain mad scientists have dreamed of holding governments hostage with doomsday plans, all in pursuit of wealth, power, fame, and a suitably terrified public. In The Wandering Earth, meanwhile, humanity takes the whole planet—and all its hopes—on a journey through the universe. But today is not about making Earth wander. We are going in the opposite direction: how might one destroy it, simply and elegantly?

  Destroying Earth is not easy. Sure, you could end human civilization, wipe out every higher life form with a super-plague, or invent nanomachines programmed to erase the entire biosphere. Yet in every case, the ground beneath our feet would survive and keep circling the Sun for billions of years. Let us be serious. If you mean to destroy the planet, the whole planet has to go.

Step One: Get the Math Right

  Earth is held together by its own gravity. Picture an enormous “onion” made of rock and magma. Gravity binds the first layer of magma to the innermost core. Their combined pull holds the next layer, whose added weight attracts the layer after that. You get the idea. The pattern repeats until it accounts for Earth’s entire mass—all 5.97×10^24 kilograms of it—and produces the gravity that keeps you in your chair instead of floating away.

  One way to destroy Earth, then, is to peel this “onion” layer by layer. Every layer, every rock, every speck of dust, and a tremendous quantity of molten magma must be launched into space. A brief trip does not count. Every last piece has to escape Earth’s gravity completely and for good.

  In other words, every discarded piece of Earth must reach escape velocity. That is no small feat. We normally need gigantic rockets just to send a spacecraft weighing a few metric tons into orbit or beyond.

  Once you get started, though, the job grows steadily easier. Every bit of matter removed lowers Earth’s mass and weakens its gravitational grip. Peel away the planet one layer at a time, and each layer becomes easier to launch than the last. We can estimate the entire job with the formula for the gravitational binding energy of a uniform sphere. It relates the energy needed to destroy—or, more politely, “liberate”—a planet to its mass and radius. For Earth, the answer is roughly 10^32 joules.

Step Two: Find an Energy Source

  That is quite a lot of energy. In all of 2013, humanity consumed a mere 10^20 joules to run everything from wood fires and engines to alarm clocks, televisions, and e-readers. Suppose you somehow seized the complete output of every nuclear, hydroelectric, and fossil-fuel power plant, every solar panel, every wind farm, and every other source—leaving nothing for anyone else. You would still have to save it for a trillion years to reach the scale we need.

  If you expect anyone to take you seriously as a planet-destroying mad scientist, you need a better plan. The Sun may swell into a red giant and engulf Earth in only about five billion years. Destroying the planet after that would rather miss the point, wouldn’t it?

  What about the Sun? It is enormous, bright, and pouring out vast amounts of energy at every moment. Our star consumes about 400 million kilograms of hydrogen in nuclear fusion reactions every second, sending the resulting energy into space as radiation. Most of it disappears without doing anything interesting or useful; only a tiny fraction reaches Earth. Billions of years ago, algae and plants learned to capture some of that sunlight through photosynthesis and use it to survive. The energy eventually travels up the food chain and into whatever you are about to eat. But will that be enough?

Step Three: Wait

  Cover Earth’s entire surface with solar panels and capture every bit of radiation that reaches it, and you would need … about 18 million years to gather enough energy to overcome the planet’s gravitational binding. That beats waiting trillions of years for human-made energy, but it is still a lengthy project. Better hope no superhero finds your secret base in the meantime.

  Then again, only a tiny fraction of the Sun’s energy ever reaches Earth. What if you could capture its entire output? Now you need just one week to collect enough energy for the job. One week! Not bad. Everyone on Earth would finally take your threats seriously. Of course, if you can build a device that captures all the Sun’s energy … why are you still hanging around on Earth?

References

1.https://www.livescience.com/64559-how-to-destroy-earth.html2.https://www.space.com/35515-six-cosmic-catastrophes-that-could-wipe-out-life-on-earth.html

entry.title: The Wandering Earth: A Brief Film Review
entry.content:
Author: 观复·钧天

  I usually prefer peace and quiet, so even sitting in a theater for a pulse-pounding science-fiction movie is a rare experience for me. Big-budget science fiction has long seemed to belong to Hollywood, and saving Earth is one of the genre’s familiar themes. I never expected China’s first homegrown science-fiction blockbuster to be this good: its logic holds up, and the story feels reasonably complete. Much of the credit must go first to the excellent framework provided by Liu Cixin’s novel.

  Once humanity begins to see itself as the master of this planet, one problem follows another. People killing one another is only the most immediate. Species extinction and humanity’s domination of the biosphere run deeper. Only when the planet we depend on can no longer support us do we realize that all our previous efforts have come to nothing. Philosophically, saving Earth means saving humanity itself—if humanity still has a soul.

  That is where the story begins. Earth breaks free of the solar system and begins to wander. “Wandering” is an extraordinarily vivid word here, at once helpless and terrifying. A makeshift team joins the effort to save the planet. During a rescue mission that seems nearly hopeless, its members must defy human institutions and even “the law” before finally pulling Earth back from the brink of destruction. It is a beautiful ideal, revealing both the compassion and the resolve of the author and the filmmakers.

  Traditional Chinese systems of knowledge did not include the methodology of experimental science in the modern sense; the modern natural sciences were introduced largely from the West. Today, nine years of compulsory education may place mathematics, physics, and chemistry near the center of the curriculum, but learning science and developing a scientific outlook are very different things. A gulf remains between reason and emotion.

  Long before our ancestors understood science, imagination gave us the myths of the Classic of Mountains and Seas: Nüwa mending the sky, Kuafu chasing the sun, and Jingwei filling the sea. Myth explains nature’s unknown origins; science fiction opens a door onto future civilizations. These stories are still told with delight in China today. Yet myth cannot simply evolve into modern science fiction, because science fiction must be grounded in scientific knowledge and logic.

  As an important starting point for industrial-scale Chinese science-fiction cinema, The Wandering Earth is far more accomplished than expected. Many of its shots can stand beside those in Hollywood blockbusters, the plot moves briskly, and the relationships among the characters are clear. Its main weakness is the lack of emotional connection between those characters. Confrontation outweighs communication, and calculation outweighs human warmth: there is blood but too little flesh, emotion but too little intimacy, despite a few genuinely moving scenes. The film avoids narrow-mindedness, but its tense passages could use more humor. The more intense a scene becomes, the more it can benefit from a measured touch of comedy—provided the jokes are actually funny.

  China was a latecomer to space exploration and to science-fiction publishing and filmmaking, but that has changed dramatically in recent years. This film has been described as the beginning of a new era in Chinese cinema, one entry in a series of ambitious and expensive productions. Before The Wandering Earth, a project of this kind was beyond the technical and financial reach of most Chinese filmmakers. It was a test of the industry itself.

  Saving Earth is an ideal. To my mind, the greatest difference between an ideal and a goal is whether it can be readily achieved. From that perspective, saving the planet is humanity’s greatest ideal precisely because it is so difficult—and because we are still willing to try.

entry.title: Gaia Reveals How Dead Sun-Like Stars Crystallize
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

  On January 9, 2019, data from Gaia, the European Space Agency’s Milky Way–mapping spacecraft, revealed for the first time how white dwarfs, the dead remnants of stars like our Sun, crystallize into solid spheres as their hot interiors cool.

  Scientists predicted the solidification, or crystallization, of matter inside white dwarfs 50 years ago. Only with Gaia, however, have astronomers been able to observe enough white dwarfs precisely enough to see the telltale pattern.

  “Before Gaia, we had distances for only a few hundred white dwarfs, and many of them were in clusters where they all had the same age,” said Pier-Emmanuel Tremblay of the University of Warwick in the United Kingdom, lead author of the study published in Nature. “With Gaia, we now have distances, brightnesses, and colors for hundreds of thousands of white dwarfs—a substantial sample across the Milky Way’s outer disk, covering a range of initial masses and ages.” Gaia’s precise distance measurements were the breakthrough, allowing astronomers to determine the stars’ true brightness with unprecedented accuracy.

Diagram of the core of a crystallizing white dwarf | Source: ESA

  On a truly cosmic scale, M100 is a magnificent grand-design spiral galaxy. It contains more than 100 billion stars and has well-defined spiral arms like those of our Milky Way. Also known as NGC 4321, M100 is one of the brightest members of the Virgo Cluster. It lies in the direction of the constellation Coma Berenices, about 56 million light-years away. This recent Hubble Space Telescope image, taken with Wide Field Camera 3, highlights the bright blue star clusters and intricate, winding dust lanes characteristic of such galaxies. Studies of variable stars in M100 have played an important role in determining the size and age of the universe.

The evolution of a star | Source: ESA

  White dwarfs are the remnants of medium-sized stars like the Sun. Once such a star exhausts the nuclear fuel in its core, it sheds its outer layers and leaves behind a hot core that slowly cools. These ultradense remnants continue to emit thermal radiation, although they appear faint to astronomers. An estimated 97% of the stars in the Milky Way will ultimately become white dwarfs, while more massive stars end as neutron stars or black holes. White dwarfs take billions of years to cool. Once they reach a certain temperature, the formerly incandescent matter in the core begins to crystallize and turn solid. The process resembles liquid water freezing at zero degrees Celsius on Earth, except that a white dwarf solidifies at the extraordinarily high temperature of roughly 10 million degrees Celsius. For this study, astronomers analyzed more than 15,000 candidate stellar remnants observed by Gaia within 300 light-years of Earth and found that the crystallizing white dwarfs formed a distinctive group.

This Hertzsprung–Russell diagram—named after the astronomers who studied stellar evolution in the early twentieth century—combines information about the brightness, color, and distance of more than 15,000 white dwarfs within 300 light-years of Earth. The black points show data from the European Space Agency's second Gaia data release. The blue lines show the cooling sequences for white dwarfs of different masses—0.6, 0.9, and 1.1 times the mass of the Sun—as predicted by theoretical models. | By analyzing Gaia's data, scientists found a concentration of white dwarfs with particular colors and brightnesses, highlighted by the orange line, that were not related through their evolutionary histories. They realized that this concentration was not a distinct population but the effect of initially hot matter inside the stellar cores cooling and crystallizing. | Source: ESA

  “We saw a concentration of white dwarfs with particular colors and brightnesses that were not related through their evolutionary histories,” Pier-Emmanuel said. “We realized that this was not a distinct population of white dwarfs, but the effect of cooling and crystallization predicted 50 years ago.” The heat released during crystallization, a process that lasts billions of years, appears to slow the evolution of white dwarfs. The dead stars stop fading and therefore look two billion years younger than they really are. That, in turn, changes our understanding of the stellar populations to which they belong. “White dwarfs are commonly used to determine the ages of stellar populations such as star clusters, the outer disk, and the Milky Way’s halo,” Pier-Emmanuel explained. “We must now develop better crystallization models to estimate the ages of these systems more accurately.”

  Not all white dwarfs crystallize at the same rate. More massive white dwarfs cool faster and reach the crystallization temperature in about one billion years. Lower-mass white dwarfs, which more closely resemble the Sun’s expected final state, cool more slowly and take six billion years to become solid spheres. The Sun has about five billion years left before it becomes a white dwarf, and astronomers estimate that it will take another five billion years after that to cool into a “crystal ball.”

  “This result highlights Gaia’s versatility and its many applications,” said Timo Prusti, ESA’s Gaia project scientist. “It is exciting that scanning the stars across the sky and measuring their properties can demonstrate the existence of plasma phenomena in matter at densities so extreme that they cannot be tested in a laboratory.”

Article Source

  1. https://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Gaia/Gaia_reveals_how_Sun-like_stars_turn_solid_after_their_demise

entry.title: A Stunning Animation of a Solar Flare
entry.content:
Author: 一毫秒的永恒

In this solar-flare visualization, purple represents plasma cooler than one million kelvins, red represents temperatures between one and ten million kelvins, and green represents temperatures above ten million kelvins.

  This animated visualization models the life cycle of a solar flare in three dimensions, using different colors to show the temperatures reached during the eruption. The magnetic-field lines dance: first they surge, then erupt, and finally settle down. Beyond producing a striking view of a solar flare, the simulation lays important groundwork for predicting flare activity in space weather.

  Solar flares are the most powerful explosions in our solar system—and spectacular events to behold. They form near sunspots, the dark patches on the Sun’s surface that are cooler than the churning plasma around them. According to NASA, sunspots form where strong magnetic fields suppress convection, cooling the local region. Loop-shaped flare structures appear when stored energy is suddenly released at the solar surface. To model a flare from beginning to end, the researchers had to calculate the energy required for one to form across the simulated region. They reported that their model extended more than 6,000 miles (10,000 kilometers) below the Sun’s surface and nearly 25,000 miles (40,000 kilometers) above it, reaching into the corona. Once they had set up the solar simulation, they let the model evolve on its own to see whether a flare would emerge naturally.

  It did.

  Although solar flares occur about 93 million miles (149 million kilometers) from Earth, they can have major effects here. Flares are sometimes accompanied by intense solar storms that hurl large quantities of charged particles and plasma into space. When that material interacts with Earth’s magnetic field, it can trigger geomagnetic storms that disrupt communications networks, power systems, and satellites. Solar storms may also interfere with animals that use Earth’s magnetic field to navigate, including migrating whales.

References

  1. https://www.space.com/43034-solar-flare-animation.html
  2. https://www.livescience.com/60326-sun-unleashes-decades-strongest-solar-flare.html

entry.title: How Long Is a Day on Saturn? Scientists Finally Have a Precise Answer
entry.content:
Author: A Millisecond of Eternity

NASA's Cassini spacecraft captured this view of Saturn's northern hemisphere as it approached summer solstice in 2016. A Saturnian year lasts 29 Earth years; according to the latest analysis of Cassini data, a day lasts just 10:33:38.

  Using new data from NASA’s Cassini spacecraft, researchers believe they have solved a long-standing mystery in solar system science: how long a day lasts on Saturn. The answer is 10 hours, 33 minutes, and 38 seconds. Planetary scientists spent decades trying to pin down that number because the rotating gas giant has no fixed surface to track and its unusual magnetic field masks its rotation rate.

  As it turns out, the answer was hidden in Saturn’s rings.

  While Cassini orbited Saturn, its instruments examined the planet’s icy, rocky rings in unprecedented detail. Christopher Mankovich, then a graduate student in astronomy and astrophysics at the University of California, Santa Cruz, used those data to study wave patterns within the rings. His work showed that the rings respond to Saturn’s own oscillations, much as a seismometer records vibrations from an earthquake. Oscillations inside Saturn cause extremely small, periodic shifts in the distribution of its mass, making the surrounding gravitational field fluctuate. The rings also respond to Saturn’s magnetic field. Mankovich explained that particles throughout the rings feel these oscillations in the gravitational field. At certain locations, the oscillations nudge ring particles at just the right moment, allowing energy to build gradually in their orbits. That energy is then carried away as observable waves.

  Mankovich’s study, published in The Astrophysical Journal on January 17, 2019, details how he developed models of Saturn’s internal structure that reproduced the waves observed in the rings. The models allowed him to trace motion inside the planet and ultimately determine its rotation period. The analysis yielded a period of 10 hours, 33 minutes, and 38 seconds, several minutes shorter than the estimate derived from Voyager radio signals in 1981.

  Voyager’s estimate was 10 hours, 39 minutes, and 23 seconds, based on magnetic-field data. Cassini relied on magnetic data as well, but its early estimates ranged from 10 hours and 36 minutes to 10 hours and 48 minutes.

  Scientists usually rely on a planet’s magnetic field to measure its rotation rate. Jupiter’s magnetic axis, like Earth’s, is not aligned with its rotation axis. As the planet spins, the magnetic axis therefore wobbles, producing a periodic radio signal from which scientists can derive the rotation rate. Saturn is different: its unusual magnetic axis is almost perfectly aligned with its rotation axis, so this method does not work. Researchers instead turned to waves in Saturn’s rings to probe the planet’s interior and pin down this long-sought fundamental property. The result delighted Saturn researchers, giving them their best answer yet to one of the planet’s most basic questions. The idea of using Saturn’s rings to study the planet’s seismology was first proposed in 1982, well before observations precise enough to do so became possible.

  Co-author Mark Marley, now at NASA’s Ames Research Center, developed the idea in detail in his 1990 doctoral dissertation. Along with presenting the calculations, he predicted where the relevant features would appear in Saturn’s rings. Marley also pointed out that the planned Cassini mission could make the observations needed to test his idea. Twenty years later, during Cassini’s final years, scientists analyzed the mission data and found ring features exactly where Marley had predicted them.

  Cassini’s mission ended in September 2017, when the mission team deliberately sent the fuel-starved spacecraft into Saturn’s atmosphere to prevent it from colliding with one of the planet’s moons. The mission was a collaboration among NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA), and the Italian Space Agency. NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) managed the mission for the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington. JPL designed, developed, and assembled the Cassini orbiter; the radar instrument was developed jointly by JPL, the Italian Space Agency, and team members from the United States and several European countries.

entry.title: A Mathematician's Sense of Beauty: Penrose Tilings
entry.content:
Author: Martin Gardner
Translator: Tu Hong
Excerpted from Fractals, Take-Away Games, and Penrose Tilings, Shanghai Scientific and Technological Education Publishing House
Text and images selected from the WeChat account Fun Mathematics (ID: mathfun)

  Sir Roger Penrose (1931– ) is a British mathematical physicist known for major work in general relativity and cosmology. He has also contributed to recreational mathematics and philosophy. This article is excerpted from Fractals, Take-Away Games, and Penrose Tilings, a volume in a classic collection of Martin Gardner’s writing on recreational mathematics.

  In 1957, Scientific American ran my column on periodic tilings of the plane by congruent convex polygons. The piece was later reprinted in Time Travel and Other Mathematical Bewilderments. At its close, I promised a future column on nonperiodic tilings. This chapter reprints the 1977 column in which I kept that promise and first presented an extraordinary nonperiodic tiling discovered by the celebrated British mathematical physicist and cosmologist Roger Penrose. I will begin with a few definitions and some background.

  A tiling is periodic if some outlined region can tile the entire plane by translation, meaning that it is moved without being rotated or reflected. The Dutch artist M. C. Escher [Translator’s note: M. C. Escher (1898–1972) was a Dutch printmaker renowned for the mathematical character of his art. His work often features tessellations, impossible structures, paradoxes, and cycles, and gives visual expression to such mathematical ideas as fractals, symmetry, hyperbolic geometry, polyhedra, and topology.] became famous for pictures made by periodically tiling the plane with shapes that resemble living creatures. The image below is a representative example. A neighboring black bird and white bird form the fundamental region of its translational tiling. Imagine laying transparent paper over the plane and tracing the outline of every tile. If the tiling is periodic, you can slide the paper to a new position, without rotating it, and make every outline coincide again.

  Infinitely many shapes, including the regular hexagon, can tile only periodically. Infinitely many others can tile either periodically or nonperiodically. A chessboard, for example, can easily be turned into a nonperiodic tiling of congruent isosceles right triangles or quadrilaterals. Bisect each square as shown at left in Figure (A) below, changing the orientation of the cuts so that no period develops. Dominoes can also form nonperiodic tilings quite easily.

  Isosceles triangles can also tile radially, as in the center of Figure (A) above. Although this tiling is highly ordered, it is plainly not periodic. As Michael Goldberg pointed out in a 1955 paper titled “Central Tessellations,” such a tiling can be cut in half and the two half-planes shifted by one or more steps to form the nonperiodic spiral shown at right in Figure (A). By replacing the two equal sides of the triangle with two congruent lines, the triangle can be distorted in infinitely many ways, as shown at left in Figure (B). If the new edges consist of straight segments, the resulting polygons—with 5, 7, 9, or 11 sides—can tile in spirals. The image below shows a striking pattern obtained in this way with a nonagon. Heinz Voderberg first discovered it by a complicated method; Goldberg’s way of deriving the figure makes it seem almost routine.

  In every known nonperiodic tiling made from congruent shapes, the same shape can also tile periodically. The right side of Figure (B) above shows two of Voderberg’s nonagons joined to form an octagon, which plainly tiles periodically.

  Another kind of nonperiodic arrangement can be produced by fitting a set of shapes together into larger copies of themselves. Solomon W. Golomb called such shapes “rep-tiles.” (See Chapter 19 of my book The Unexpected Hanging.) The image below shows how the shape known as the “sphinx” produces a nonperiodic tiling by generating ever-larger sphinxes. As in the preceding example, two sphinxes—one rotated 180°—can tile periodically in an obvious way.

  Do any sets of tiles admit only nonperiodic tilings? Here “only” means that no single shape, no subset, and not even the set as a whole can tile periodically, although the full set can tile nonperiodically. Rotations and reflections are allowed.

  For decades, experts believed that no such set existed, but the conjecture proved false. In 1961, Hao Wang [Translator’s note: Hao Wang (1921–1995) was a Chinese American philosopher and mathematical logician. He held posts at Harvard University, the University of Oxford, and Rockefeller University, and also served as a research engineer at the Burroughs Corporation, a technical expert at Bell Telephone Laboratories, and a visiting scientist at the IBM Research Center, among other roles.] became interested in tiling the plane with sets of unit squares whose edges were colored in different ways. These unit squares are known as Wang tiles. Wang also wrote an excellent 1965 article about them for Scientific American. His problem was to find a method for determining whether any given set of tiles could cover the plane so that adjacent edges always had matching colors, with rotations and reflections forbidden. The problem matters because it is connected to decision problems in symbolic logic. Wang conjectured that every set of tiles capable of covering the plane could do so periodically. He also proved that if this were true, a decision method for such tilings would exist.

  In 1964, Robert Berger proved Wang’s conjecture false in his Harvard doctoral dissertation in applied mathematics. No universally applicable method exists, and therefore there is a set of Wang tiles that can tile only nonperiodically. Berger constructed such a set from more than 20,000 tiles. He later found a much smaller set of 104, and Donald Knuth [Translator’s note: Donald Knuth (1938– ) is a celebrated American computer scientist. He created the field of algorithm analysis and invented the TeX typesetting system and the Metafont type-design system. His Chinese name, Gao Dena, was chosen before his visit to China in 1977.] reduced the number to 92.

  A set of Wang tiles can readily be converted into polygonal tiles that force nonperiodicity. Replace the colored edges with matching protrusions and indentations, as on jigsaw pieces, so that the polygons fit only where the colors previously matched. An edge that bore one color can then fit only an edge that bore the same color, and likewise for every other color. Allowing rotations and reflections, Raphael M. Robinson constructed six tiles that force aperiodic tilings in the sense described above (see the image below). In 1977, Robert Ammann [Translator’s note: Robert Ammann (1946–1994) was an American amateur mathematician who made several important contributions to the theory of quasicrystals and aperiodic tilings.] found a different set of six tiles that does the same. It remains unknown whether the number of square tiles can be reduced below six, though there is good reason to think six is the minimum.

  Penrose was Rouse Ball Professor of Mathematics at the University of Oxford. There he discovered several small sets of nonsquare tiles that force nonperiodicity. Although most of his work concerns relativity and quantum mechanics, he has maintained an active interest in recreational mathematics. He shared that pleasure with his father, the late geneticist L. S. Penrose. Together they invented the famous “Penrose stairs,” a staircase that loops endlessly without ever climbing higher. Escher depicted it in his print Ascending and Descending. In 1973, Penrose discovered a set of six tiles that forces aperiodic tilings. In 1974, he found a way to reduce the set to four. Soon afterward, he reduced it again, to two.

  Because the tiles were suitable for commercial puzzle games, Penrose did not agree to make them public until he had applied for patents in Britain, the United States, and Japan. Those patents remain in force today. I am equally indebted to Conway for many results he obtained while studying Penrose tilings.

  The shapes of a pair of Penrose tiles can vary, but the most interesting pair is the “dart” and “kite,” as Conway named them. Figure (A) below shows how both shapes can be obtained from a rhombus with interior angles of 72 and 108 degrees. Divide the long diagonal in the familiar golden ratio, (1＋√5)/2＝1.61803398…, [Editor’s note: In China, the golden ratio is generally written as (√5-1)/2＝0.618…, while it is generally written abroad as (1＋√5)/2＝1.618…. The two are reciprocals; only the order of the ratio differs.] and connect that point to the two obtuse vertices. It is that simple. Let φ denote the golden ratio. As the figure shows, every line segment has length either 1 or φ. The smallest angle is 36 degrees, and every other angle is a multiple of it.

  The rhombus can, of course, tile periodically, but Penrose tiles are not allowed to meet in that fashion. Equal-length edges must not match indiscriminately. Protrusions and indentations could enforce the restriction, but simpler devices work as well. One is to label each vertex H for “head” or T for “tail,” as shown in Figure (B), and permit joined edges only when like-labeled vertices meet. Two colors of dots at the vertices make this rule easier to follow. Conway proposed a more elegant device: draw two colors of arcs on each tile, shown in black and gray in the illustration.
